boston-roxbury-grant-lawsuit-2026.excerpt: The city says the U.S. Department of Transportation unlawfully withdrew a 2022 award for safety, transit and accessibility work on three major corridors.
boston-roxbury-grant-lawsuit-2026.text: boston sues over $20m grant for roxbury street upgrades the city says the u.s. department of transportation unlawfully withdrew a 2022 award for safety, transit and accessibility work on three major corridors. the city of boston has gone to federal court to recover a $20 million transportation grant that officials say was withdrawn after the project included a small electric-vehicle charging component. the lawsuit, filed sept. 28 in the u.s. district court for the district of massachusetts, asks the court to reverse the u.s. department of transportation's cancellation of the 2022 award for the roxbury resilient corridors project. the filing and case number, city of boston v. duffy, are listed in the public docket record (https://dockets.justia.com/docket/massachusetts/madce/1:2026cv14419/306825). the dispute centers on three roxbury streets: melnea cass boulevard, malcolm x boulevard and warren street. boston's project page says the grant was intended to support street repairs, safer crossings, transit improvements, accessibility work, traffic-flow changes, trees, lighting, public spaces and stormwater features. the city describes the corridors as central roadways in a historically disinvested neighborhood and says the project was being developed with local residents and community organizations (https://www.boston.gov/departments/transportation/project/roxbury-resilient-corridors). according to a sept. 28 announcement from u.s. rep. ayanna pressley and mayor michelle wu, the city argues that dot cited the project's electric-vehicle charging infrastructure as the reason for canceling the entire award. the announcement says that charging work represented less than 1% of project costs and that federal transportation officials had previously encouraged the city to include it. those are the city's allegations about the cancellation; the lawsuit has not produced a merits ruling (https://pressley.house.gov/2026/09/28/pressley-wu-announce-lawsuit-against-trump-administration-to-protect-20-million-federal-grant-for-roxburys-street-improvements/). the guardian independently reported that the case names transportation secretary sean duffy and was filed against the department over its decision to withdraw the money. the newspaper also reported the city's position that federal agencies cannot rewrite a program established by congress to match changing political priorities. the department's response was not included in the sources reviewed for this report, so the federal government's legal defense and any timetable for responding remain unclear (https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/28/boston-sues-trump-administration). the stakes are practical for people who use roxbury's busiest routes. boston says the project is meant to improve bus service, walking, bicycling and driving conditions at the same time. on its warren street project page, the city says more than 20,250 mbta riders use that corridor each weekday and that delays can add as much as 20 minutes to an average rider's day. that page predates the lawsuit and describes the broader transit problem rather than measuring the effect of the canceled grant, but it helps explain why the city treats the award as more than a budget line (https://content.boston.gov/departments/transportation/project/warren-street-bus-priority-corridor). roxbury's transportation history also shapes the argument. boston says the wide, vehicle-oriented corridors were created through eminent-domain and block-clearance decisions during the urban-renewal era of the 1960s. the city's current plan calls for safer crossings, more comfortable bus stops, shade and cooling spaces, bike infrastructure and green stormwater measures, while also trying to prevent displacement and support small businesses. those goals remain proposed project features, not completed improvements. the case arrives after the city had already approved accepting the federal award. a boston city council record from april 2025 describes the $20 million raise grant as funding to reconstruct and upgrade the three roxbury corridors. the city now says the cancellation removed a major share of the money needed to move the work forward. whether the court restores the award, sends the decision back to dot for reconsideration or leaves the cancellation in place will determine what boston can realistically build and when (https://content.boston.gov/departments/city-council/city-council-roll-call-votes?page=39). for now, the lawsuit is an opening filing, not a ruling that boston has won or that dot acted unlawfully. the public docket shows the case was assigned to u.s. district judge richard g. stearns after an initial judge recused himself on the filing date. the next meaningful developments will be the federal defendants' response, any request for interim relief and the court's decision on how the administrative procedure act claims proceed. until then, the three-corridor project remains listed by boston as pending, with its completion year undetermined. massachusetts massachusetts massachusetts ma boston roxbury, boston massachusetts boston roxbury transportation federal grants public transit ct-21st-cclc-after-school-grants-2026-10.excerpt: The three-year federal grant package will support 25 programs serving schools in communities including Bridgeport, Hartford, New Haven, Stamford and Waterbury, with another 11 recipients planned for 2027–28.
ct-21st-cclc-after-school-grants-2026-10.text: connecticut directs $15 million to expand after-school programs across the state the three-year federal grant package will support 25 programs serving schools in communities including bridgeport, hartford, new haven, stamford and waterbury, with another 11 recipients planned for 2027–28. connecticut is committing about $15 million over three years to expand after-school learning, mentoring and enrichment programs, the state department of education announced oct. 7. the federal 21st century community learning center awards will fund 25 programs beginning oct. 1, 2026, and are aimed at students in schools with high concentrations of low-income students. the first-year awards total $4,905,155, according to the department’s published recipient table. the grants reach a broad group of school districts and community organizations. current-year recipients include programs in bridgeport, bristol, east hartford, hartford, hamden, killingly, manchester, meriden, middletown, new london, norwalk, stamford, torrington and waterbury. awards range from $94,349 for a carver program serving side by side charter school in norwalk to $227,500 for several projects, including programs in bridgeport, hamden and waterbury. the state received 55 applications and says the awards were selected through a competitive review. the money is designed to extend the school day rather than simply provide child care. the [u.s. department of education’s program description](https://www.ed.gov/grants-and-programs/formula-grants/school-improvement-grants/nita-m-lowey-21st-century-community-learning-centers-title-iv-part-b) says 21st century community learning centers support academic enrichment in reading, math and other subjects, along with broader activities and family educational services during non-school hours. connecticut’s announcement lists tutoring, science and technology, mentoring, arts, athletics, wellness, cultural programs and family engagement among the possible uses. the local structure matters because the grant does not create one statewide after-school schedule. districts and nonprofit lead applicants will operate the programs, identify participating students and decide how to fit activities around their school communities. in torrington, for example, [edadvance says its bases program uses 21st cclc funding](https://bases.edadvance.org/grantsandpartners) for sites at torrington intermediate school and torrington middle school. that kind of school-by-school arrangement means families will need to look to their district or provider for enrollment rules, hours, transportation and the exact services available. the department is also reserving roughly $2.1 million for 11 additional recipients in a three-year cohort scheduled to begin in the 2027–28 school year. those planned awards include programs connected to schools in bristol, east hartford, groton, middletown, new haven and waterbury. the future cohort is separate from the 25 programs starting this fall, and the department says both federal funding and compliance with program requirements must continue for the awards to remain in place. the federal grants are part of a larger connecticut after-school investment. the state says it is separately providing about $5.3 million for 41 programs during the 2026–27 school year, bringing the combined annual state and federal investment to about $10 million. those figures describe funding streams, not the number of children served. the oct. 7 release does not provide a statewide enrollment total, a common attendance target or a single measure that will show whether the new programs improve academic outcomes. that unanswered implementation question will shape the program’s regional impact. the awards put new resources into communities where schools and families may need supervised time, academic support and enrichment beyond regular hours, but the value will depend on staffing, participation and continuity. the immediate change is that local organizations have funding authority and named school sites; the next step is for them to publish schedules and turn the grants into programs families can actually use. connecticut education education ct hartford ct-bottle-deposit-law-penalties-2026-10-.excerpt: A new statute bars people from collecting Connecticut refunds on containers bought elsewhere and allows misdemeanor or felony charges when the volume reaches thousands of bottles or cans.
ct-bottle-deposit-law-penalties-2026-10-.text: connecticut bottle-deposit law adds criminal penalties for large out-of-state redemptions a new statute bars people from collecting connecticut refunds on containers bought elsewhere and allows misdemeanor or felony charges when the volume reaches thousands of bottles or cans. connecticut's latest bottle-deposit changes took effect oct. 1, adding criminal penalties to the state's effort to stop people from redeeming large quantities of beverage containers that were purchased somewhere else. [public act 26-148](https://www.cga.ct.gov/2026/act/pa/pdf/2026pa-00148-r00sb-00457-pa.pdf) says no person may collect or charge a refund value on a container not purchased in connecticut, and it applies to conduct the law describes as willful. the statute sets escalating criminal categories by volume. willfully redeeming 5,000 to 19,999 out-of-state containers in a calendar year is a class b misdemeanor under the act. the law identifies 20,000 to 30,999 containers during a one-year period as a class a misdemeanor, and 40,000 or more as a class d felony. the published act does not state a separate threshold in the text between 31,000 and 39,999 containers, an omission that could matter if prosecutors try to apply the new scale to a case in that range. the law is aimed at a problem that grew after connecticut raised its standard deposit from five cents to 10 cents in january 2024. connecticut is one of a small group of states with bottle-return programs, while neighboring rhode island has no cash-deposit system and new york generally uses a five-cent deposit. that difference can create an incentive to bring containers across a state line and collect connecticut's higher refund, even though the deposit was never paid here. [ct insider](https://www.ctinsider.com/connecticut/article/bottle-deposit-law-changes-october-1-22441604.php) reported oct. 3 that connecticut's redemption rate rose sharply after the 10-cent deposit began, then declined as other controls took effect. the [connecticut department of energy and environmental protection](https://portal.ct.gov/deep/reduce-reuse-recycle/bottles/connecticut-bottle-bill) reported an 85.7% rate for the first quarter of 2026 and 79.6% for the quarter ending june 30, according to the report. those figures show how many containers were redeemed, but they do not identify how many returns were fraudulent or how many came from outside the state. the new criminal provision is one part of a broader regulatory response. [deep's bottle-bill guidance](https://portal.ct.gov/deep/reduce-reuse-recycle/bottles/connecticut-bottle-bill) says redemption-center owners and operators must obtain a state license beginning july 1, 2026, and submit a $2,500 fee with the application. earlier changes also created identification and record-keeping requirements for high-volume returns and set daily limits. the rules are designed to give the state more information about who is redeeming containers and how much material passes through each center, although enforcement still requires investigators to connect a person to a large number of containers and show that the conduct was willful. the law specifically exempts common or contract carriers and warehouse workers who are lawfully transporting or storing beverage containers as merchandise, along with employees acting within that job. that language distinguishes ordinary shipping and distribution from the conduct the statute targets. it also means the new penalties are not a blanket ban on moving beverage containers across state lines; the issue is collecting connecticut's refund on containers that were not bought in connecticut. the dispute has consequences beyond people waiting in redemption-center lines. [ct insider](https://www.ctinsider.com/connecticut/article/bottle-deposit-law-changes-october-1-22441604.php) described beverage distributors as absorbing handling and refund costs when redemption volumes exceed the number of containers sold in the state. a bridgeport redemption-center owner told the publication that new scanning equipment could change how quickly his employees process returns and could affect staffing. connecticut's challenge is to reduce cross-border abuse without making legitimate recycling harder for consumers, charities and businesses that depend on the deposit system. [deep](https://portal.ct.gov/deep/reduce-reuse-recycle/bottles/connecticut-bottle-bill) has said the bottle bill remains an environmental program as well as a financial one: deposits are intended to keep containers out of roads, waterways and landfills and to feed usable material back into manufacturing. the oct. 1 law therefore starts another phase of a policy experiment that connecticut began when it doubled the deposit. state officials will have to see whether licensing, identification, scanning and the new criminal thresholds stabilize redemption rates without shifting too much cost onto redemption centers or ordinary residents. connecticut connecticut connecticut ct hartford connecticut connecticut bottle bill recycling environmental policy consumer protection

ct-bridgeport-dennis-bradley-absentee-ba.excerpt: State prosecutors say Dennis Bradley opened a voter’s completed ballot and directed her to change a vote in the August probate-judge primary; he was released and is due in court Oct. 21.
ct-bridgeport-dennis-bradley-absentee-ba.text: former connecticut senator charged in bridgeport absentee-ballot case state prosecutors say dennis bradley opened a voter’s completed ballot and directed her to change a vote in the august probate-judge primary; he was released and is due in court oct. 21. former connecticut state sen. dennis a. bradley jr. has been charged in an investigation into the handling of an absentee ballot during bridgeport’s august democratic primary, putting a new criminal case at the center of the city’s long-running debate over election safeguards. the [connecticut division of criminal justice](https://portal.ct.gov/dcj/press-releases/division-of-criminal-justice/10062026bradley?language=en_us) announced the charges oct. 6 and said bradley was released on a promise to appear in bridgeport superior court on oct. 21. the state says bradley, 42, of bridgeport, faces two counts of illegal possession of absentee ballots and envelopes, a charge alleging that he was present when an absentee-ballot applicant executed a ballot, and a charge under connecticut’s absentee-ballot law. the state’s release identifies the statutes as general statutes sections 9-140b(d), 9-140b(e) and 9-359. those are charging documents and allegations, not findings that bradley committed the conduct. the division of criminal justice explicitly said he is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court. the investigation grew out of the aug. 11 democratic primary for bridgeport judge of probate. incumbent paul ganim faced challenger mark bradley, dennis bradley’s brother. according to the state, a woman contacted bridgeport police on aug. 5 and the state elections enforcement commission, or seec, on aug. 6. she alleged that a man she knew as dennis bradley came to her apartment, opened an absentee ballot she had already completed, and instructed her to change her vote from ganim to mark bradley. seec referred the matter to the office of the chief state’s attorney for further investigation. the [ct post’s report](https://www.ctpost.com/news/article/bridgeport-ct-dennis-bradley-ballot-arrest-22465181.php) said bradley turned himself in at troop g in bridgeport after a warrant was signed. his attorney, darnell crosland, told the newspaper that bradley maintains his innocence, called the allegations “paper thin,” and said his client was working as a canvasser for the bradley for probate campaign. crosland said he negotiated the surrender and confirmed the oct. 21 arraignment date. bradley could not immediately be reached for comment, the ct post reported. wfsb separately reported that the arrest was announced by chief state’s attorney patrick j. griffin and that bradley was charged and released. that account also said the case concerns the same primary contest and that investigators received the initial complaint before the seec referral. the consistent point across the official release and the independent reports is narrower than the political arguments surrounding the race: prosecutors have filed charges over alleged ballot handling, but the underlying account remains to be tested through the criminal process. the timing gives the case significance beyond the individuals involved. connecticut began issuing absentee ballots for the nov. 3 general election on oct. 2, according to the [secretary of the state’s absentee-voting guidance](https://portal.ct.gov/sots/election-services/voter-information/absentee-voting). the state says voters can request ballots without a specific excuse under expanded access rules, while campaign workers and others who distribute or handle election materials remain subject to detailed legal requirements. a criminal case involving a former elected official may therefore affect how campaigns, voters and election administrators talk about the boundaries around completed ballots during the final weeks of the 2026 election. bridgeport has faced repeated scrutiny over absentee-ballot practices in recent municipal contests. the ct post reported that bradley is already scheduled for a dec. 3 sentencing hearing in a separate federal wire-fraud case tied to his 2018 state senate campaign. that prior conviction is not proof of the new allegations, and the absentee-ballot charges are a separate proceeding. the immediate next checkpoint is the oct. 21 court appearance, where the case can move from the arrest and charging stage into formal court proceedings and where the defense can respond to the state’s allegations. connecticut connecticut connecticut ct bridgeport bridgeport, connecticut connecticut bridgeport absentee ballots election integrity state politics dennis bradley criminal justice

ct-bridgeport-porter-rally-2026-10-05.excerpt: About 60 residents, clergy, elected officials and retired officers rallied for Chief Roderick Porter as union complaints and an outside review keep pressure on Bridgeport’s police leadership.
ct-bridgeport-porter-rally-2026-10-05.text: bridgeport rally backs police chief as union calls for his removal about 60 residents, clergy, elected officials and retired officers rallied for chief roderick porter as union complaints and an outside review keep pressure on bridgeport’s police leadership. a public split over bridgeport’s police leadership widened over the weekend when residents, faith leaders, elected officials and retired officers rallied in support of police chief roderick porter. the oct. 3 gathering outside the city’s government center drew about 60 people, according to the [connecticut post](https://www.ctpost.com/news/article/bridgeport-leaders-rally-for-chief-roderick-porter-22461046.php), while members of the police union continue to call for porter’s removal. the rally was organized by former bridgeport detective harold dimbo and city council member mary mcbride-lee. speakers described porter as accessible and engaged with neighborhoods, and several supporters said his presence in the community has built trust. the [ct mirror](https://ctmirror.org/2026/10/05/bridgeport-ct-police-chief-roderick-porter-rally/) reported that residents and retired officers also framed the event as a defense of reforms that have shaped the department’s relationship with black officers and the wider community. the show of support does not resolve the complaints from inside the department. afscme local 1159 president michael salemme told the connecticut post that union leaders view the rally as a small political event and continue to point to complaints and lawsuits involving porter. the ct mirror reported that salemme cited more than 20 complaints filed by officers with the state commission on human rights and opportunities, along with several federal lawsuits. those allegations have not been adjudicated by the rally or by the news reports, and they should not be treated as findings of misconduct. the central dispute is now moving on two tracks. union representatives have sought an investigation into porter’s leadership and working conditions, while mayor joe ganim has agreed to hire an outside investigator but has declined to remove the chief. the connecticut post reported that ganim has continued to support porter, citing the department’s public-safety record, even as critics press for a change in command. neither the mayor nor the union has announced a final result from the review. porter did not attend saturday’s event, but he told the ct mirror he appreciated the community support and connected it to relationships built during his career and tenure as chief. he became a bridgeport officer in 1993 and was appointed chief in 2022, according to the connecticut post. the rally also highlighted an internal divide among members and former members of the bridgeport guardians, a minority-officer organization: some current union-aligned critics have opposed porter, while retired guardian members at the event defended him. that divide matters because bridgeport’s police department is both a public-safety agency and one of the city’s most visible institutions. questions about working conditions, discrimination claims, overtime management and leadership accountability can affect morale inside the force, public confidence outside it and the city’s exposure to legal costs. but the available reporting does not establish that any one side’s account is complete, and the size of saturday’s rally cannot measure the views of the city as a whole. the next meaningful test will be the outside review and any public response from the mayor, union and police department. until that process produces findings, the confirmed facts are narrower: supporters rallied for porter, union leaders continue to seek his removal, and bridgeport’s administration has chosen an investigation over an immediate change in command. residents and officers are therefore watching the same unresolved question from opposite sides—whether the chief’s record represents needed reform or a workplace crisis that requires new leadership. connecticut public-safety public safety ct bridgeport bridgeport government center, bridgeport, connecticut connecticut bridgeport police roderick porter police unions local government public safety

ct-business-registrations-startups-2026-.excerpt: The state recorded 50,573 business registrations through September, up from 46,402 during the same period last year. Economists say the increase may reflect both entrepreneurial opportunity and pressure in an uncertain economy.
ct-business-registrations-startups-2026-.text: connecticut business registrations climb 9% as residents test new income paths the state recorded 50,573 business registrations through september, up from 46,402 during the same period last year. economists say the increase may reflect both entrepreneurial opportunity and pressure in an uncertain economy. connecticut recorded about 50,573 business registrations during the first nine months of 2026, up from 46,402 in the same period of 2025. that is an increase of 4,171 registrations, or about 9%. the figures, reported by [the hour](https://www.thehour.com/business/article/new-business-registrations-ct-jobs-employment-22473845.php), offer a timely look at how connecticut residents and companies are responding to a labor market shaped by high costs, technology changes and uncertainty. the comparison comes from the state’s business-registry data rather than an estimate of jobs or economic output. the [connecticut business registrations dataset](https://data.ct.gov/business/connecticut-business-registrations-2018-present/mk5y-yz6u), maintained by the secretary of the state’s office, lists monthly totals for entities registered in connecticut. adding the january-through-september totals produces 50,573 for 2026 and 46,402 for 2025. the dataset was updated oct. 11, so the comparison does not include october’s full results. the registry is broad. connecticut’s open-data documentation says it covers domestic businesses formed in the state as well as foreign businesses created elsewhere that register to operate in connecticut. that means the increase should not be read as 4,171 new storefronts, employers or full-time jobs. it is a measure of filings and registrations, including activity that may involve a new company, an expansion into the state or a change in how an owner organizes work. the reasons behind the increase are also mixed. the hour reported that david cadden, professor emeritus at quinnipiac university, viewed the numbers as evidence that some people are trying to create an independent source of income before a job loss or other disruption forces the issue. brian marks, a senior lecturer at the university of new haven, pointed to the combination of economic pressure and new technology as making it easier for people to pursue side work, contract work or a small business while keeping another job. that interpretation matters in connecticut because a registration can be both a sign of confidence and a defensive move. someone may be building a product or service because demand looks promising, but another person may be formalizing gig work after finding that a regular paycheck no longer covers housing, health care, transportation or other expenses. the filing itself does not reveal which situation applies, and the state data does not identify the owner’s reason for registering. artificial intelligence is part of the new-business discussion as well. the hour cited ethan mollick, a university of pennsylvania associate professor who studies innovation and entrepreneurship, on the way ai can handle routine tasks and let a small operator focus on a narrower specialty. the same reporting noted a limit that is important for new businesses: ai systems can produce confident but incorrect work, so owners still need to check research, contracts, financial assumptions and customer-facing claims before relying on the output. for people considering a filing, the state’s [business.ct.gov service](https://business.ct.gov/) provides registration information, entity guidance and a new-business checklist. the [secretary of the state’s office](https://portal.ct.gov/sots) also maintains business records and related services. those resources can make the administrative step easier, but they do not guarantee financing, customers, licensing approval or a profitable operation. the next useful question is whether the registration growth turns into durable businesses and jobs. monthly filings can show whether the 2026 pace continues, while employment, tax, closure and survival data would show whether the new entities are contributing lasting economic activity. for now, the clearest verified conclusion is narrower: more business entities are being registered in connecticut than last year, and experts see the rise as a combination of opportunity, technology and economic self-protection rather than a single statewide boom. connecticut business business ct connecticut statewide connecticut business registrations entrepreneurship small business gig economy artificial intelligence economic trends

ct-cheapr-bev-rebate-increase-2026-10-15.excerpt: The CHEAPR increase takes effect Oct. 15, while additional rebates remain available for income-qualified buyers and residents of environmental-justice communities.
ct-cheapr-bev-rebate-increase-2026-10-15.text: connecticut raises standard rebate for new battery-electric vehicles to $1,500 the cheapr increase takes effect oct. 15, while additional rebates remain available for income-qualified buyers and residents of environmental-justice communities. connecticut is increasing the standard point-of-sale rebate for a new battery-electric vehicle from $1,000 to $1,500 on thursday, a change state officials say is intended to lower the upfront cost of cleaner transportation as buyers face higher vehicle prices and the loss of a federal incentive. the connecticut department of energy and environmental protection announced the change oct. 14 for the connecticut hydrogen and electric automobile purchase rebate, known as cheapr. the higher amount applies to an eligible vehicle purchased or leased on or after oct. 15, according to deep. the standard program is open to connecticut licensed drivers who buy or lease an eligible new vehicle from a licensed connecticut new-car dealer or an eligible original equipment manufacturer. deep’s program materials set a $50,000 price cap for new vehicles and describe the standard rebate as a point-of-sale credit, meaning the approved amount is applied through the purchase or lease transaction rather than handled as a later state tax filing. the increase does not change every cheapr incentive. the standard rebate for a new plug-in hybrid remains $500. for buyers who qualify for rebate+, the additional voucher for a new battery-electric vehicle remains $3,000, bringing the combined new-bev incentive to $4,500. the rebate+ add-on for a new plug-in hybrid remains $1,500, for a combined $2,000. rebate+ incentives for used vehicles also remain unchanged at $5,000 for a battery-electric vehicle and $3,000 for a plug-in hybrid, according to deep’s updated program page. rebate+ is targeted rather than automatic. a connecticut driver must be prequalified and meet at least one of the program’s criteria: living in an environmental-justice community or distressed municipality, participating in a qualifying state or federal income-support program, or having household income below 300% of the federal poverty level. the [cheapr rebate+ guidance](https://portal.ct.gov/deep/air/mobile-sources/cheapr/cheapr---rebate-plus) says people seeking the new-vehicle add-on must apply for a voucher before buying or leasing and provide that voucher to the dealer. private sales are not eligible for the used-vehicle rebate+ incentive. deep said the policy is a response to a sharp change in the electric-vehicle market. demand for cheapr surged in 2025 before the federal tax credit expired on oct. 1 of that year, prompting the state to reduce its standard rebate. the agency said rebates have fallen by half since the federal credit ended and pointed to tariffs, manufacturing costs and vehicle availability as additional pressures. returning the standard new-bev amount to $1,500 is meant to narrow that affordability gap, although it does not restore the larger federal benefit that connecticut buyers previously could have combined with state help. the program is already a statewide transportation and air-quality policy, not just a discount for early adopters. deep said cheapr has helped almost 28,000 drivers obtain an electric vehicle and issued more than $50 million in rebates since the program began in 2015. the department also reported more than 2,700 new-ev incentives since the start of 2026, including more than 520 rebate+ awards. the [center for sustainable energy](https://energycenter.org/program/connecticut-hydrogen-and-electric-automobile-purchase-rebate-program), which administers cheapr, describes it as the nation’s first statewide point-of-sale ev rebate program and reported nearly $48.7 million in issued or reserved rebates as of april 2026; the different totals reflect different reporting dates and program accounting. the stakes reach beyond the transaction at a dealership. deep says connecticut has more than 2.7 million registered vehicles, with cars and trucks responsible for almost 70% of smog-forming emissions and nearly 35% of the state’s climate pollution. the agency reported that connecticut’s air exceeded federal ozone standards on 17 days in 2026, compared with 22 days in 2025 and 23 days in 2024. those figures are the department’s rationale for treating vehicle incentives as an air-quality tool, while the immediate household benefit depends on the price, financing, charging access and operating needs of each vehicle buyer. for residents considering a purchase, the practical sequence is to confirm that the vehicle appears on the current cheapr eligible list, ask the dealer to process the standard rebate, and complete rebate+ prequalification before signing if the household may qualify. the u.s. department of energy’s [alternative fuels data center](https://afdc.energy.gov/laws/all?state=ct) says cheapr awards are first-come, first-served. deep said it will continue monitoring demand and work with the cheapr board and general assembly on future program changes, so the amounts and available funding remain subject to later state decisions. connecticut environment environment ct hartford connecticut connecticut electric vehicles cheapr ev rebates clean transportation air quality consumer costs

ct-college-clery-rape-reports-2025.excerpt: New Clery reports show wide differences among Connecticut campuses, but the figures count reports rather than proven crimes and cannot be used as a simple safety ranking.
ct-college-clery-rape-reports-2025.text: connecticut colleges reported more than 100 rapes in 2025, campus data shows new clery reports show wide differences among connecticut campuses, but the figures count reports rather than proven crimes and cannot be used as a simple safety ranking. connecticut colleges and universities recorded more than 100 reports of rape in calendar year 2025, according to a review of newly released campus security reports. the figures span incidents reported to schools, campus security authorities, police and other designated officials, and they cover campus property, some school-controlled locations away from campus and certain nearby public areas. they are a record of reports, not a statewide count of prosecutions or a finding that every reported allegation was substantiated. the numbers were compiled in an oct. 7 [ct insider review](https://www.ctinsider.com/news/education/article/campus-crime-reports-rape-ct-universities-2025-22462715.php) of annual security reports required under the federal jeanne clery disclosure of campus security policy and campus crime statistics act. the reports are released each year by colleges that participate in federal student-aid programs. the law is intended to make campus crime and safety information public, but its categories and geography are narrower than a general measure of all sexual violence affecting students. a small group of schools accounted for much of the total. ct insider’s compilation lists 37 reported rapes at the university of hartford, 27 at yale university and 13 at trinity college. it lists six each at connecticut college, the university of new haven and eastern connecticut state university, with smaller totals at several other institutions. yale’s reports were all categorized as occurring in student dormitories or other residential facilities. the yale total rose from 19 in 2024 but remained below the 56 reported in 2023, according to the university’s report as summarized by ct insider. the university of hartford’s [2026 annual security and fire safety report](https://www.hartford.edu/student-life/public-safety/%5ffiles/2026-uhartford-annual-security-and-fire-report-final-9.30.2026.pdf) records 37 rape reports for 2025, including 36 in student housing. the report says a significant number resulted from one report and that an outside investigation found insufficient information to proceed. that explanation does not erase the report from the clery count, but it does show why a high number cannot by itself establish how many separate assaults occurred or compare one campus fairly with another. the university of connecticut provides another example of why the data needs context. in its [release about the 2025 clery report](https://today.uconn.edu/2026/09/uconn-releases-annual-safety-reports-8/), uconn says its count includes information from more than 1,200 campus security authorities, such as resident assistants, coaches and faculty advisers. the university also says it records reports even when details are incomplete or a third party makes the disclosure. ct insider’s review lists three reported rapes at uconn’s storrs campus, while uconn’s release describes two sexual-assault reports there, a difference that underscores how category labels and reporting rules can affect comparisons. other campuses reported few or no rapes in the same year. ct insider lists no reported rapes at wesleyan university or quinnipiac university, while southern connecticut state university, central connecticut state university and western connecticut state university each reported one or two. those figures should not be read as proof that no sexual violence occurred. the [connecticut alliance to end sexual violence](https://endsexualviolencect.org/) told ct insider that clery reports are a limited snapshot because many survivors do not report, and different campuses may have different levels of awareness, trust and access to reporting channels. a separate [wfsb report](https://www.wfsb.com/2026/10/05/yales-sexual-violence-reports-far-exceed-other-ct-schools-police-point-location/) found that yale’s numbers were much higher than those at most connecticut schools and quoted new haven police pointing to the university’s location near a midsize city as one factor that may influence reports. that is a possible explanation, not a conclusion about any individual case or campus. the clery reports do not supply enough information to determine why one school’s numbers differ from another’s. for students and families, the practical value of the reports is transparency rather than a league table. they identify what schools were told, where reports were categorized and what prevention, response and support policies campuses say they maintain. the next useful questions are whether students know how to report, whether confidential and non-police options are available, how institutions explain unusual statistical changes and what resources are offered regardless of whether a complainant seeks an investigation. the 2025 data makes those questions more visible across connecticut, but it does not answer them on its own. connecticut education education ct-convertible-pistol-ban-injunction-202.excerpt: A preliminary injunction pauses Connecticut’s new sales and import ban while Glock and industry plaintiffs challenge the law under the Second Amendment.
ct-convertible-pistol-ban-injunction-202.text: federal judge blocks connecticut convertible-pistol ban before it can take effect a preliminary injunction pauses connecticut’s new sales and import ban while glock and industry plaintiffs challenge the law under the second amendment. a federal judge has temporarily blocked connecticut from enforcing a new law that would prohibit the sale, importation and distribution of certain semiautomatic pistols that can be converted into fully automatic weapons. the preliminary injunction came sept. 30, hours before public act 26-41 was scheduled to take effect, and leaves the law in place while the constitutional challenge moves forward. the u.s. district court order covers two related cases brought by glock inc. and a group that includes the national shooting sports foundation, shadow systems and blue trail range corporation. judge kari a. dooley did not strike down the statute or decide every question raised by the plaintiffs. instead, she found for purposes of the preliminary-injunction request that the plaintiffs were likely to succeed on their second amendment claim, were likely to suffer irreparable harm without immediate relief, and had satisfied the other requirements for an injunction. the order says the court is preserving the status quo until the issues can be developed and adjudicated more fully. the law, house bill 5043 during the legislative process, defines a convertible pistol as a semiautomatic pistol with a cruciform trigger bar that can be changed by hand or with a common household tool through the attachment of a pistol converter. the law’s definition excludes some hammer-fired pistols and some designs with a shielded trigger bar. for covered pistols manufactured on or after oct. 1, a person or business that distributes, transports, imports, keeps for sale or offers one for sale would face a class d felony under the statute. connecticut’s [official description of the law](https://portal.ct.gov/governor/news/press-releases/2026/06-2026/governor-lamont-signs-legislation-prohibiting-the-sale-of-pistols-that-can-easily-be-converted) says the measure targets firearms that can be altered with illegal conversion devices; it does not legalize those devices or converted machine guns. the dispute turned on how the second amendment’s historical test applies to a law aimed at a firearm that is legal in its ordinary, unmodified form. the defendants pointed to founding-era “proving laws” from pennsylvania, new jersey, new hampshire and massachusetts that required firearm inspections or manufacturing standards before sale, along with the longstanding regulation of machine guns. the plaintiffs argued that the historical tradition addresses illegal modifications and converted weapons rather than banning a common semiautomatic handgun because someone might later misuse it. dooley wrote that the state’s proposed historical comparisons did not adequately rebut the presumption that the law was unconstitutional at this early stage. the order distinguishes safety inspections before a firearm enters commerce from efforts to prevent future misuse after a firearm has been sold. it also notes that the parties did not dispute that unconverted handguns with cruciform trigger bars are safe and popular for self-defense. the judge cautioned that the result could change after a fuller record is developed. the ruling has immediate practical consequences for connecticut gun dealers and manufacturers. the court cited evidence that blue trail range had about $25,000 worth of affected handguns and had stopped ordering new inventory because of the law. the plaintiffs also argued that the statute could disrupt contracts, advertising and sales to law-enforcement customers who were not exempted. those business and customer claims helped support the court’s finding of irreparable harm, but they remain part of an ongoing lawsuit rather than a final judgment on the statute’s validity. connecticut attorney general william tong has said the state will defend the law, calling its gun-safety provisions lawful and lifesaving. [connecticut public](https://www.ctpublic.org/news/2026-10-02/judge-pauses-ct-ban-on-the-sale-of-guns-that-can-be-turned-into-quick-firing-weapons) reported that the injunction blocks the law from taking effect while the case proceeds. the next phase will determine whether the state can produce a stronger constitutional justification, whether the plaintiffs’ claims survive further litigation and whether the injunction remains in place. until a later court order changes the situation, the sales ban is paused; the separate prohibition on conversion devices and converted machine guns remains in force. connecticut connecticut connecticut ct bridgeport connecticut connecticut courts firearms law second amendment gun policy

ct-cscu-leadership-accountability-2026-1.excerpt: A succession of departures and investigations has left CSCU relying on interim leaders while state officials debate whether the problem is individual conduct, the system's structure, or both.
ct-cscu-leadership-accountability-2026-1.text: connecticut public college system faces leadership reset as accountability debate widens a succession of departures and investigations has left cscu relying on interim leaders while state officials debate whether the problem is individual conduct, the system's structure, or both. connecticut's public college system is entering a new phase of leadership uncertainty after a series of high-level departures, investigations and governance disputes. a [ct insider report](https://www.ctinsider.com/news/education/article/cscu-leadership-accountability-lamont-fazio-22455854.php) published oct. 6 said the connecticut state colleges and universities system is navigating vacancies and several interim leaders while officials argue over who is responsible for restoring public confidence. the stakes are statewide. cscu serves about 100,000 students through connecticut's four state universities, connecticut state community college and its 12 campuses, and charter oak state college, according to ct insider and a [connecticut mirror overview](https://ctmirror.org/2026/05/26/natalie-braswell-named-interim-chancellor-of-cscu-system/). leadership disruption at the system office therefore reaches far beyond one campus: it affects the institutions that educate workers, train nurses and teachers, and provide lower-cost transfer routes for students across the state. the recent sequence began with the departure of former chancellor terrence cheng after state scrutiny of spending and expense practices, followed in april by the resignation of interim chancellor o. john maduko while he was under investigation over allegations of sexual harassment and inappropriate workplace conduct. ct mirror reported on both the resignation and the system's decision to place general counsel karen buffkin on paid leave amid questions about how the complaint was handled. those allegations were not criminal findings, and the personnel actions did not by themselves establish every claim made about the officials. the turmoil deepened in september. an independent review by grand river solutions found serious failures in the system's handling of the maduko matter and faulted multiple officials, according to the current ct insider report. on sept. 23, central connecticut state university president zulma toro announced her resignation after administrators raised allegations of bullying and intimidation. [ct mirror reported](https://ctmirror.org/2026/09/23/ccsu-zulma-toro-resigns-bullying-allegations/) that cscu said the concerns were serious but that its investigation into toro would not continue after her resignation and retirement; the report did not establish that the allegations were proven. that same day, board of regents vice chair juanita james resigned, citing what she described as a dysfunctional culture and political infighting, ct insider reported. the departures have produced an argument that is partly about personnel and partly about design. connecticut created the consolidated system in 2011 by bringing its community colleges, regional state universities and online college under a board of regents and central office. supporters have said a statewide structure can make transfers and shared services easier; critics question whether concentrating authority at the top makes it harder to detect problems and assign responsibility. former cscu president mark ojakian offered the counterargument in a [connecticut public interview](https://www.ctpublic.org/news/2026-06-17/major-leader-of-ct-higher-ed-consolidation-effort-breaks-silence-to-defend-cscu-system), saying the recent scandals reflected individual leadership failures rather than proof that consolidation itself was broken. faculty and other critics have pointed to repeated executive turnover and long-running funding pressure as evidence that the structure also deserves review. those are competing interpretations, not settled findings, and the distinction matters as officials consider changes that could affect every public college in the state. interim chancellor natalie braswell has said the system will announce reforms involving compliance, leadership vetting and governance in the coming weeks. ct insider reported that the board of regents has 15 voting seats, with appointments divided among the governor, legislative leaders and students, and that five seats were vacant at the time of the report. the arrangement gives several institutions a role in oversight, but it can also blur the answer to a basic public question: who must act when a concern crosses from a campus office into system leadership? the immediate next steps are the search for a permanent chancellor, decisions about interim leadership at affected institutions and the promised governance proposals. legislative leaders have indicated that cscu-related legislation is likely when the general assembly returns in january. for students and employees, the practical test will be whether those steps produce clearer reporting channels, credible investigations and stable leadership without interrupting campus services. the system has acknowledged the need for accountability; the coming months will show whether that promise becomes a durable change in how connecticut's public colleges are run. connecticut education education ct new britain connecticut state colleges and universities, statewide connecticut higher education cscu central connecticut state university board of regents governance accountability

ct-danbury-white-supremacist-rally-2026-.excerpt: Police say they learned of the brief Oct. 3 demonstration only after it ended; the gathering followed Danbury’s vote to open police applications to lawful permanent residents and DACA recipients.
ct-danbury-white-supremacist-rally-2026-.text: danbury officials condemn masked white-supremacist rally outside police headquarters police say they learned of the brief oct. 3 demonstration only after it ended; the gathering followed danbury’s vote to open police applications to lawful permanent residents and daca recipients. a masked group carrying a “keep new england white” banner demonstrated outside danbury police headquarters saturday night, prompting condemnations from city and state officials and a statement from the police chief. the gathering was documented in video and confirmed by danbury police after the group had left, according to the stamford advocate’s oct. 5 report: https://www.stamfordadvocate.com/news/article/white-supremacist-group-danbury-police-22462288.php. the video showed roughly a dozen people on a public sidewalk near the department, some wearing face coverings. local reporting said people in the group could be heard shouting white-supremacist slogans and making nazi-style salutes. police spokesperson erin henry told the stamford advocate that officers were not aware of the demonstration while it was happening and had no interaction with the participants. chief patrick ridenhour said the department confirmed the footage was authentic and stressed that the demonstrators were not police employees. ridenhour said the department cannot control who uses a public sidewalk outside its building, but he rejected the group’s message as inconsistent with the department’s mission. he said danbury police do not support or condone organizations that promote hate or exclusion and are committed to protecting everyone in the city. the police department had not announced arrests or criminal charges in the reporting available monday, and the length of the demonstration was not clear. mayor roberto alves said danbury has no place for hate, racism or white supremacy and described the city’s racial, religious and cultural diversity as a strength. in an interview with public-radio station wshu, alves said the participants appeared to arrive briefly and disperse quickly, and that police were investigating. wshu’s report, published oct. 5, also included the perspective of carolina bortoletto of danbury united for immigrants, who said the demonstration was intended to frighten an immigrant community: https://www.wshu.org/connecticut-news/2026-10-05/ct-danbury-mayor-white-power-rally. the demonstration came weeks after the danbury city council voted 18-2 to change the eligibility rules for police applicants. the ordinance now permits lawful permanent residents and recipients of deferred action for childhood arrivals, or daca, to apply. the change did not remove the department’s other screening requirements, including background, medical, psychological, physical and drug testing. the city’s published ordinance says applicants must also complete the required connecticut police training and pass a competitive civil-service process: https://www.danbury-ct.gov/documentcenter/view/6916/meeting-notice-and-packet---pd-ordinances-sec-22-19-thru-22-30--42826?bidid=. the timing and stated target of the rally were reported by danbury patch, which said northeast action claimed responsibility in a telegram post and connected the demonstration to the council’s hiring decision. patch also reported that the counter extremism project has described northeast action as a neo-nazi organization and said the group claims activity across connecticut and other northeastern states. those descriptions come from the reporting and outside group assessments; northeast news has not independently verified the organization’s membership or the authenticity of every online post: https://patch.com/connecticut/danbury/neo-nazi-group-targets-danbury-after-police-hiring-change. the incident has raised a local question that extends beyond one brief protest: how public agencies protect free expression in public spaces while responding to intimidation aimed at residents or public employees. danbury officials have condemned the message, but the available reports do not describe arrests, injuries or property damage. the city and police have not publicly identified participants, and it remains unclear whether the investigation will produce any charges or additional public-safety measures. for residents, the immediate facts are limited but clear. the demonstration occurred outside the police headquarters on oct. 3, police learned of it after it ended, officials confirmed the video and publicly rejected the group’s message. any further response will depend on what investigators can establish about the participants, their conduct and whether any law was violated. connecticut public-safety public safety ct danbury danbury police headquarters, danbury, connecticut connecticut danbury danbury police department white supremacy hate groups immigration ct-east-hampton-power-surge-2026-10-14.excerpt: Eversource crews and firefighters are checking wiring before service returns after a suspected equipment malfunction left residents without power and prompted smoke calls.
ct-east-hampton-power-surge-2026-10-14.text: east hampton power surge leaves 41 homes awaiting electrical inspections eversource crews and firefighters are checking wiring before service returns after a suspected equipment malfunction left residents without power and prompted smoke calls. eversource crews and east hampton firefighters are going door to door after a possible power surge affected 41 homes in the connecticut town, leaving residents waiting for electrical inspections before service can safely return. town officials said the incident followed an eversource equipment malfunction tuesday night, oct. 13, but the company and town have not described a final technical cause. the affected area includes hog hill road, terp lane and schoolhouse lane, according to [wfsb’s report](https://www.wfsb.com/2026/10/14/power-surge-may-have-damaged-wiring-east-hampton-homes-town-says/). the immediate concern is not simply the loss of electricity. officials said the voltage event may have damaged wiring or circuits inside individual houses, creating a risk that power could be restored to a damaged system. the inspection process is therefore being handled home by home rather than as a routine outage repair. eversource told wfsb that extensive testing of electrical equipment in the affected homes was required before service could safely resume. east hampton town manager david cox told wfsb that at least 19 people called 911 tuesday night after noticing some smoke inside their homes. the report said officials did not believe the damage was widespread, but at least one house had circuit problems that would require significant electrical work. those details remain preliminary: the sources do not report a confirmed fire, injuries or a complete accounting of property damage. the inspections can take time because crews must check the electrical system in each home. [wtic news reported](https://www.audacy.com/wtic/news/local/east-hampton-power-surge-and-door-to-door-home-inspections) that residents were being asked to unplug equipment and remove lightbulbs from fixed fixtures while circuit panels were tested, a process that can take about an hour per house. the town identified terp road, higher-numbered addresses on schoolhouse lane and numbers 70 through 128 on hog hill road as areas where residents should expect visits, according to wfsb. eversource said it was working to restore service to the 41 customers near hog hill road while coordinating with town officials and residents. the company’s public statement did not give a restoration deadline. town officials said small groups of homes could be reconnected after they were cleared, while some properties might need another inspection after power returned. that means the neighborhood may not come back online all at once. residents also received a warning about generators. eversource asked people in the affected area to leave generators off until the wiring had been checked. that instruction matters because a generator connected to a damaged electrical system can create additional hazards for occupants and utility workers. homeowners who believe equipment or wiring was damaged were told they could use an electrician and submit a claim to eversource; the company’s position, as described by the town and [the hour](https://www.thehour.com/news/article/east-hampton-power-surge-electrical-damage-22476288.php), is that internal wiring damage initially falls to the property owner while the claim is reviewed. the incident is a different kind of outage from a storm-related line failure. in a conventional interruption, a utility can often repair the fault and re-energize a circuit after confirming that the outside network is safe. here, the reported surge or back-feed may have reached equipment inside homes, so crews must account for conditions beyond the utility pole. the public reports do not yet say which component malfunctioned, how high the voltage rose or whether every affected house sustained damage. for east hampton residents, the next milestones are the completion of the house-by-house tests, a safe restoration schedule and clearer information about reimbursement. the town and eversource were still investigating wednesday, oct. 14, and the available reports did not establish whether the event was isolated to the three named roads or whether additional customers could later be identified. until inspections are complete, residents should follow the utility and local officials’ instructions about generators, electrical equipment and access for repair crews. connecticut utilities utilities ct east hampton east hampton, connecticut connecticut east hampton eversource power outage electrical safety utility damage homeowners

ct-energy-efficiency-ranking-2026-10-14.excerpt: WalletHub placed Connecticut 26th nationally and behind every other New England state in a ranking that combines household and vehicle energy-use measures.
ct-energy-efficiency-ranking-2026-10-14.text: connecticut ranks last among new england states in new energy-efficiency study wallethub placed connecticut 26th nationally and behind every other new england state in a ranking that combines household and vehicle energy-use measures. connecticut ranked last among the six new england states in wallethub’s [2026 energy-efficiency study](https://wallethub.com/edu/most-and-least-energy-efficient-states/7354), a result that puts a fresh number on the region’s debate over utility costs, home heating and transportation. the study placed connecticut 26th among the 48 states it evaluated, while vermont ranked second nationally, massachusetts fifth, maine 12th, rhode island 14th and new hampshire 22nd. alaska and hawaii were excluded because of data limitations, according to wallethub. the ranking is not a direct scorecard of connecticut’s climate policy or a finding that every home in the state uses more energy than homes elsewhere. wallethub combined two dimensions: home energy efficiency and auto energy efficiency. its home measure compares residential energy consumption per person with annual heating and cooling degree days, an adjustment intended to account for different weather conditions. the auto measure incorporates vehicle-fuel efficiency and miles driven per person. connecticut’s overall score was 57.94. the state ranked 31st in home energy efficiency and 16th in auto energy efficiency. those component rankings help explain why the overall result can look different from assessments focused on public programs or building policy: the wallethub formula gives home and auto efficiency equal weight, while its underlying data also reflect how much people drive and how much energy homes consume relative to local weather. the study was released oct. 13 using data collected through sept. 15 from the u.s. census bureau, the national climatic data center, the u.s. energy information administration and the federal highway administration. wallethub said the purpose was to compare how much energy states use in homes and vehicles, not to estimate an individual household’s bill or determine which state has the lowest utility prices. that distinction matters for connecticut residents heading into the heating season. [the connecticut post](https://www.ctpost.com/business/article/connecticut-energy-efficiency-wallethub-ranking-22475557.php), which reported on the ranking oct. 14, noted that the u.s. department of energy estimates energy-efficiency measures can reduce household utility costs by as much as 25 percent. the savings available to a particular household will depend on the building, heating system, weather, driving patterns and the cost of the work, so the national ranking does not predict what any one resident will pay. energy experts quoted by the connecticut post pointed to relatively low-cost steps such as weather stripping, insulation, led bulbs and low-flow shower heads. they also discussed heat pumps as a possible way to combine heating and cooling efficiency, depending on a home’s location and existing system. a home energy audit can help identify which improvements are likely to provide the best return rather than treating every upgrade as equally useful. connecticut already operates a statewide efficiency system through [energize connecticut](https://www.energizect.com/eeb-statewide-energy-efficiency-dashboard), an initiative involving the state, utilities and the connecticut green bank. the program says its rebates, consultations and other services are funded through charges on electric and natural-gas bills and are guided by the energy efficiency board and regulated by the public utilities regulatory authority. its public dashboard tracks participation, spending and other program measures, giving residents a separate way to evaluate the state’s efficiency efforts. the next question is how state programs and household decisions translate into future rankings and lower bills. wallethub’s study does not identify a single cause for connecticut’s position, and it does not measure every factor that shapes energy affordability, such as utility rate design, housing age or access to financing. what it does show is a regional contrast: vermont and massachusetts scored near the top nationally, while connecticut’s combined home-and-auto result lagged the rest of new england. connecticut energy energy ct connecticut statewide connecticut energy ct-fall-turkey-firearms-season-2026-10-0.excerpt: The season runs Oct. 3 through Oct. 31, while a new state rule clarifies when small-game and turkey hunters need landowner permission.
ct-fall-turkey-firearms-season-2026-10-0.text: connecticut fall firearms turkey season opens with updated permission rules the season runs oct. 3 through oct. 31, while a new state rule clarifies when small-game and turkey hunters need landowner permission. connecticut’s fall firearms turkey season opens saturday, oct. 3, and runs through oct. 31, the department of energy and environmental protection announced friday. the opening applies to eligible state and private lands, while the state’s pheasant and broader small-game seasons are scheduled to begin oct. 17. fall archery seasons for deer and turkey began sept. 15, giving connecticut hunters several overlapping ways to use the state’s forests and private landscapes this month. [deep’s opening notice](https://portal.ct.gov/deep/news-releases/news-releases---2026/deep-announces-opening-days-of-fall-turkey-pheasant-and-small-game-hunting-seasons) describes the firearms opener as part of the agency’s annual schedule and urges hunters to participate safely and responsibly. the basic turkey rules are specific. the fall firearms bag limit is three turkeys of either sex on private land, state land or a combination of the two. hunting hours begin one-half hour before sunrise and end at sunset. connecticut residents need a firearms hunting license and a resident game bird conservation stamp. nonresidents need either a three-day out-of-state bird-hunting license or a nonresident firearms license, along with the stamp. the state’s [2026 wild-turkey guide](https://portal.ct.gov/deep/hunting/2026-connecticut-hunting-and-trapping-guide/wild-turkey-hunting) says shotguns must be 20 gauge or larger, use no. 4 through no. 7 1/2 shot or a permitted combination, and be limited to three shells. access rules matter as much as the season dates. a hunter on private land must carry signed written consent from the landowner on deep’s official form for the current season. turkey hunting is allowed on sundays only on private land, and sunday hunting cannot take place within 40 yards of a blazed public trail. hunters using state land should check deep’s interactive hunting-area map because not every state property is open to fall firearms turkey hunting. decoys are allowed, but live decoys are prohibited. the 2026 season also arrives with a permission change that took effect oct. 1. deep says verbal permission is sufficient for small-game hunting on private land every day of the week, including sundays. deer and turkey hunters still need written permission from private landowners. the agency also says the legal definition of a muzzleloader has changed: the projectile must be loaded from the muzzle end. those distinctions are important for people moving between small-game, deer and turkey seasons, because permission requirements do not apply identically to each activity. deep’s safety guidance focuses on preventing a person from being mistaken for a bird. hunters should remain in a fixed location and call turkeys to them rather than stalk a turkey or a turkey call. before firing, they should identify the target and what lies beyond it. the guide recommends sitting with protection from an approaching hunter, such as a tree at least as wide as the hunter’s shoulders, and placing a four- to six-inch fluorescent-orange band around the tree about six feet above the ground to identify the calling position. hunters should not wear red, white, blue or black while turkey hunting, and deep recommends fluorescent orange while walking to and from the hunting area and when carrying a harvested bird. harvest paperwork continues after a successful hunt. a hunter must immediately complete and sign a harvest tag and keep it with the turkey until the carcass is cut up for consumption. deep also requires deer and turkey harvests to be reported within 24 hours through its online hunter reporting website or by calling 1-877-337-4868, according to the agency’s [fall archery season notice](https://portal.ct.gov/deep/news-releases/news-releases---2026/fall-archery-deer-and-turkey-season-opens-in-september). the reporting requirement gives wildlife managers information for monitoring harvest and managing connecticut’s turkey population. for people sharing the woods, the opening changes the mix of activity on public properties beginning this weekend. hikers and other visitors should pay attention to posted notices and avoid entering closed or restricted areas, while hunters need to confirm the property rules before setting up. deep’s guide includes the season dates, license requirements, map links and landowner forms in one place. the next major statewide opening is oct. 17, when pheasant and several small-game seasons begin; closing dates vary by species. new-england new-england new england ct connecticut connecticut hunting season wild turkey outdoor safety deep

ct-flood-sba-loans-2026-10-06.excerpt: The federal designation covers Fairfield, New Haven and Litchfield counties; a Bridgeport center opens Oct. 7, with physical-damage applications due Dec. 1.
ct-flood-sba-loans-2026-10-06.text: connecticut flood survivors can seek sba loans after september disaster declaration the federal designation covers fairfield, new haven and litchfield counties; a bridgeport center opens oct. 7, with physical-damage applications due dec. 1. people whose homes, belongings or businesses were damaged by connecticut’s sept. 13 flash flooding can begin applying for low-interest federal disaster loans after the u.s. small business administration approved a disaster declaration for fairfield county and the contiguous connecticut counties of new haven and litchfield. gov. ned lamont announced the designation tuesday. the [connecticut governor’s office](https://portal.ct.gov/governor/news/press-releases/2026/10-2026/governor-lamont-secures-sba-disaster-declaration-for-september-13-flooding) said joint assessments by federal, state and local officials found damage above the threshold for sba assistance. the declaration reaches several groups at once. the governor’s office says homeowners may seek up to $500,000 to repair a primary residence, while homeowners and renters may qualify for up to $100,000 to replace damaged or destroyed personal property. businesses can apply for up to $2 million for physical losses involving real estate, inventory, machinery and equipment. businesses and private nonprofits may also seek economic injury disaster loans of up to $2 million for working capital while normal operations are disrupted. the limits are maximum loan amounts, not automatic awards. applicants still have to submit information to the sba and qualify under the agency’s disaster-loan rules. the [federal register notice](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/10/06/2026-20472/administrative-declaration-of-a-disaster-for-the-state-of-connecticut) describes the action as an administrative declaration issued oct. 2 for severe storms and flash flooding. it lists fairfield as the primary county and new haven and litchfield as contiguous connecticut counties, and sets interest rates that vary by applicant type and whether the applicant has credit available elsewhere. that distinction matters for residents trying to understand what has been approved. this announcement opens an sba loan ct-hartford-schools-forensic-audit-2026-.excerpt: A state-ordered review did not find evidence of misappropriation, but auditors said missing records, turnover and opaque budget practices limited what they could determine about the district’s recurring deficits.
ct-hartford-schools-forensic-audit-2026-.text: hartford schools audit finds no fraud but exposes deep weaknesses in budgeting and oversight a state-ordered review did not find evidence of misappropriation, but auditors said missing records, turnover and opaque budget practices limited what they could determine about the district’s recurring deficits. a forensic audit of hartford public schools found no evidence of fraud or misappropriation, but it also found that the district’s financial systems were too inconsistent and incomplete to give leaders a clear account of how recurring budget problems developed. the connecticut state department of education released the review wednesday after cliftonlarsonallen llp presented its findings to the state board of education. the result is not a clean bill of financial health. the audit examined the district’s fiscal years 2024 and 2025 and found weaknesses in budgeting, financial reporting, record retention, governance and internal controls. auditors said those conditions reduced transparency and limited their ability to determine the precise causes and magnitude of some variances and deficits. [the connecticut education department’s release](https://portal.ct.gov/sde/press-room/press-releases/2026/state-releases-hartford-public-schools-fiscal-years-2024-and-2025-forensic-audit-report) links to the full report and describes the review’s limits. cliftonlarsonallen said it used available financial records, system data, supporting documents and interviews, but could not fully reconstruct all financial activity from the two years. the firm cited significant turnover among district leaders and finance personnel, inconsistent historical records, incomplete email productions and other documentation gaps. those limitations matter because they prevent the audit from answering every question about individual transactions or assigning a single, definitive cause to the district’s financial difficulties. the report identified 14 key observations. among them, budget transfers and expenditure reclassifications were used frequently to address account-level deficits, making it harder to see the operating reasons behind budget changes. some costs were recorded in accounts that did not accurately describe their nature, while public budget materials, munis data and other reports did not always present comparable information. the auditors said revised budgets shown to the board did not consistently make clear how spending compared with the originally approved budget. the audit also pointed to management and oversight problems. department leaders reported limited involvement in final budget decisions and limited access to current financial information. board members generally understood their responsibility to approve the budget and monitor district finances, the report said, but their understanding of transfer requirements, finance committee duties and related policies was not consistent. the findings describe control weaknesses, not proof that any particular official acted improperly. other observations involved grants, purchasing and employee and vendor records. grant-funded programs were not always separated clearly from ordinary operating activity or reassessed when grant support ended. procurement documentation was not always readily available at the transaction level. auditors also found duplicate contact information in employee and vendor records and matches between active employees and vendors who received payments. cliftonlarsonallen said those matches do not by themselves indicate fraud or improper relationships, but they should be reviewed for legitimate explanations, disclosures and compliance with conflict-of-interest and procurement rules. the findings arrive after hartford schools reported a projected multimillion-dollar shortfall and state officials expanded their intervention. nbc connecticut reported that the state board ordered the audit after the district reported a deficit of about $29 million for the 2026-27 school year. [nbc’s report](https://www.nbcconnecticut.com/news/local/no-misuse-of-funds-found-in-hartford-public-schools-forensic-audit/3782798/) also noted the distinction between the absence of identified misuse and the continuing budget problems. wfsb reported that auditors could not fully review some activity because records were missing or incomplete and that special education, transportation and lost grant funding were among the district’s major cost pressures. [its oct. 8 report](https://www.wfsb.com/2026/10/08/hartford-schools-audit-finds-no-fraud-cites-financial-oversight-weaknesses/) said the recommendations call for better expense tracking, stronger board oversight and tighter record-keeping. cliftonlarsonallen issued 33 recommendations for the district and eight more for the board of education. the state says implementing them would improve transparency, accountability and financial stewardship. the review is not finished: fiscal year 2026 information was not sufficiently final for definitive findings, and the auditors will begin that work after hartford completes its year-end closeout. for families, employees and taxpayers, that next phase will be important because the newly released audit identifies why the district’s records were difficult to trust without yet resolving the full scale or origin of the latest deficit. connecticut education education ct hartford hartford, connecticut connecticut hartford hartford public schools education forensic audit school finance state oversight
