ct-head-start-overhaul-opposition-2026-1.text: connecticut leaders oppose proposed head start overhaul as comment period closes gov. ned lamont, attorney general william tong and early-childhood commissioner elena trueworthy say proposed federal changes could weaken standards serving about 5,600 connecticut children and families. the public-comment period closed tuesday. connecticut’s top early-childhood officials are asking the trump administration to withdraw a proposed rewrite of the federal head start rules, putting the state in direct opposition to a plan whose public-comment period closed tuesday, oct. 6. gov. ned lamont, attorney general william tong and office of early childhood commissioner elena trueworthy announced their position tuesday and said connecticut submitted written comments to the u.s. department of health and human services. the [connecticut governor’s office](https://portal.ct.gov/governor/news/press-releases/2026/10-2026/governor-lamont-urges-trump-administration-to-withdraw-proposal-to-overhaul-head-start) described the proposed rule as a broad reduction in federal performance standards. the [federal register notice](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/08/07/2026-16134/reducing-federal-burden-for-head-start-programs) says the administration for children and families wants to replace the standards last revised in 2024, reduce federal administrative requirements and defer to state policies where possible. the notice sets oct. 6 as the deadline for public comments; it does not make the proposal final. the changes under debate reach into the daily operation of head start and early head start. connecticut officials said the proposal would reduce requirements covering teaching and learning, staffing, group size, coaching and professional development. it would also remove some suspension and expulsion protections and lower the allowable administrative-cost cap from 15% to 5% of a program’s approved costs. the federal notice frames those changes as a way to reduce bureaucracy and move more resources toward direct services, while acknowledging that programs may need to change how they allocate money and staff. the local stakes are substantial even though the rule would be written in washington. the governor’s office says head start serves about 5,600 connecticut children from birth through age 5 and their families. the program includes preschool for children ages 3 to 5, early head start for infants and toddlers, services for pregnant women and home-visiting options. a [connecticut mirror report](https://ctmirror.org/2026/10/02/head-start-1002/) citing the state office of early childhood’s 2024-25 data counted 4,847 children and pregnant women participating in 34 federally funded programs, a measure that uses a different population and reporting period than the governor’s current estimate. supporters and opponents describe the tradeoff differently. hhs has said the proposal would expand access, reduce unnecessary federal bureaucracy and give local providers more flexibility, while retaining requirements for health, disability, family and school-readiness services, according to ct mirror. connecticut advocates and lawmakers argue that loosening class-size, staffing and disability-service rules could make it harder for programs to provide consistent care, particularly to children with disabilities, children experiencing homelessness or housing instability, children in foster care and families who face language or other access barriers. [wfsb’s report](https://www.wfsb.com/2026/10/06/state-leaders-push-back-proposed-head-start-changes/) said state leaders were urging residents to weigh in before the deadline. the timing also intersects with connecticut’s own expansion of early-childhood programs. lamont’s office said the state deposited $411.7 million in surplus funds into a new early childhood education endowment in june, bringing its value above $700 million. the state’s early start ct program is scheduled to expand in july 2027, with free care planned for eligible families earning up to $100,000 and a 7% household-income contribution cap for some families above that level. state officials say weaker federal head start standards could create gaps in a system connecticut is trying to build out. nothing in tuesday’s announcement changes head start services immediately. the federal agency must first review the public record and decide whether to revise, withdraw or finalize the proposed rule. connecticut’s letters call for preserving federal standards while pursuing narrower ways to reduce paperwork. until hhs takes that next step, the practical question for families and providers is not whether the overhaul has taken effect, but how the final rule will treat the staffing, language, disability and family-support requirements that make head start more than a preschool program. connecticut education education ct hartford connecticut connecticut head start early childhood education federal policy

ct-heating-assistance-12-7-million-2026-.text: connecticut adds $12.7 million to heating aid as fuel costs rise the supplemental state money will support the connecticut energy assistance program, with deliverable-fuel households able to receive aid together before the winter heating season intensifies. connecticut is adding $12.7 million in state money to its home-heating assistance program as officials prepare for higher fuel costs and a larger group of households seeking help this winter. gov. ned lamont announced the funding tuesday from the state’s federal cuts response fund, saying it will supplement federal low income home energy assistance program dollars flowing through the connecticut energy assistance program, or ceap. the [governor’s announcement](https://portal.ct.gov/governor/news/press-releases/2026/10-2026/governor-lamont-releases-state-aid-for-home-heating-assistance) identifies the money as supplemental aid for the 2026–27 season. the immediate effect is for households that use deliverable fuels such as heating oil, kerosene or propane. connecticut social services commissioner andrea barton reeves said the added funding will let eligible deliverable-fuel households receive their ceap benefits at the same time rather than waiting until one benefit is exhausted before accessing another. that timing matters in a state where a family can face a large fuel delivery bill before the coldest part of winter, particularly when the household has little room in its budget for a sudden price increase. the state’s approved federal fiscal-year 2027 plan anticipates serving about 94,291 connecticut households, including roughly 32,893 households using deliverable fuel, according to the governor’s office. the program gives priority to households with someone age 60 or older, a child younger than 6, or a person with a disability. connecticut officials told [wfsb](https://www.wfsb.com/2026/10/13/state-releases-millions-additional-heating-aid-winter-approaches/) that the assistance program has about $73 million in federal liheap funding and that roughly 10,000 additional households are now eligible, bringing the statewide total above 94,000. that larger caseload is arriving alongside a sharper cost problem. wfsb reported that heating oil was more than $2.50 per gallon higher than a year earlier and that electric costs had also risen. the station reported that state officials do not consider the $12.7 million sufficient to cover the entire shortfall, and that federal dollars will be used before the state draws on additional money. the state says about $250.6 million will remain in the federal cuts response fund after this proposal, but the amount available is not the same as money already committed to heating aid. ceap applications for the 2026–27 season are already open. the [department of social services program page](https://portal.ct.gov/dss/economic-security/winter-heating-assistance/energy-assistance---winter-heating?language=en-us) lists benefit amounts of $355 to $705, depending on household size, income and heating source. it says benefits are generally paid directly to a utility or fuel vendor, and that eligible deliverable-fuel households may qualify for additional deliveries, payment-matching plans, shut-off protection and heating-equipment repairs or replacement. income eligibility is based on annual gross income at or below 60% of connecticut’s state median income. for federal fiscal year 2027, the governor’s office lists $93,681 for a family of four; households receiving certain means-tested benefits, including snap, temporary family assistance or supplemental security income, may qualify through categorical rules. eligibility is determined through the program, so the income threshold should not be treated as an automatic award amount. residents can apply online at [ct.gov/heatinghelp](https://ct.gov/heatinghelp), through their local community action agency by phone, email or mail, or by appointment in person. connecticut says applicants should apply each year rather than assume a prior ceap award carries over. people who need help locating the right agency can call 2-1-1. the first day for program-paid fuel deliveries is nov. 2, 2026, and the application deadline for this heating season is may 31, 2027. the funding is a response to an immediate affordability squeeze, not a guarantee that every household facing a larger bill will be covered. ct-high-dosage-tutoring-grants-2026-10-0.text: connecticut sends $2 million in math tutoring grants to 42 education agencies the state says the new awards will extend intensive, curriculum-linked math support into grades 6 through 10 during the 2026-27 school year. connecticut is directing $2 million to 42 local education agencies for high-dosage mathematics tutoring, a state investment that expands the program into grades 6 through 10 during the 2026-27 school year. the [connecticut state department of education](https://portal.ct.gov/sde/press-room/press-releases/2026/connecticut-state-department-of-education-awards-%242-million-in-high-dosage-tutoring-grants) announced the awards on oct. 5 after receiving 70 applications. the department said the full amount available through the competitive grant round will go to local agencies. the awards reach districts and regional or charter-school organizations across the state. the published list includes bridgeport, danbury, hartford, stamford and waterbury, each receiving $50,000, along with smaller awards for places such as middletown, preston, regional school district 11 and southington. the list also includes education service organizations such as aces and eastconn. those awards do not by themselves establish how many students each agency will serve; local plans and implementation details will determine the reach of the tutoring. connecticut initially used nearly $11.5 million in federal american rescue plan elementary and secondary school emergency relief funding to launch high-dosage tutoring in mathematics for students in grades 6 through 9. the new round is funded through the state’s fiscal 2027 budget and moves the upper grade boundary to 10. the [department’s program overview](https://portal.ct.gov/sde/covid19/acceleratect/high-dosage-tutoring) describes the change as a continuation of the earlier effort rather than a separate, unrelated initiative. the state’s definition of high-dosage tutoring is more specific than a conventional after-school homework session. the model calls for tutoring multiple times a week, one-on-one or small-group instruction, a consistent tutor, lessons aligned with grade-level mathematics and integration into the school day when possible. the [competitive grant notice](https://portal.ct.gov/sde/rfp/request-for-proposals/2026-rfps) says the grants are intended to help agencies use those evidence-based guidelines to accelerate learning and address gaps that worsened during the pandemic. the department says the earlier program produced measurable gains for participating students, but that figure is a state-reported program result rather than an independent evaluation of the new awards. on smarter balanced assessments, csde says students who received the tutoring saw proficiency rates rise by about 9 percentage points and mathematics achievement increase by about 9 scale-score points. the announcement does not say that every district, grade or student will experience the same result, and the new grants will need to be tracked as local programs get underway. the new awards also put a statewide policy choice into practice. connecticut lawmakers created a high-dosage tutoring matching-grant program in the 2026 session, and the department’s current round uses that authorization to keep targeted math support in place after the one-time federal relief that helped start the program. that matters for districts that built tutoring around the earlier funding but still face uneven mathematics performance and limited time during the regular school day. for families, the immediate question is not how to apply for a state check. the money is going to school systems and other local education agencies, which will decide how to schedule tutoring, identify students and hire or train tutors within the state’s guidelines. the oct. 5 announcement names the awardees but does not publish a single statewide enrollment date or a common family application. parents and caregivers will therefore need to watch their district or school communications for details about eligibility, timing and whether tutoring will be offered during the school day, an intervention period or another scheduled block. the next test will be implementation. connecticut has committed the money and identified the agencies, but the public release leaves several operational questions open, including how many students will participate, how districts will report attendance and whether the gains cited from the earlier program will hold across the expanded grades. the new grants give schools another tool for mathematics recovery; their regional impact will become clearer as agencies turn the awards into recurring small-group instruction and publish results from the 2026-27 school year. connecticut connecticut connecticut ct hartford ct-housing-costs-poverty-2026-10-06.excerpt: The analysis says above-average rents are tied to 26% of child poverty in the state, putting housing supply and zoning at the center of the affordability debate.
ct-housing-costs-poverty-2026-10-06.text: connecticut housing costs account for 21% of poverty, pew analysis finds the analysis says above-average rents are tied to 26% of child poverty in the state, putting housing supply and zoning at the center of the affordability debate. above-average housing costs account for 21% of poverty in connecticut and 26% of child poverty, according to a new analysis by [the pew charitable trusts](https://www.pew.org/en/research-and-analysis/articles/2026/09/29/the-housing-shortage-is-a-major-driver-of-poverty). the findings put a familiar connecticut complaint—high rent and too few available homes—into a broader measure of household hardship: housing costs are not only squeezing budgets, but also pushing some families below a poverty threshold that adjusts for local expenses. the analysis examines 2023 housing costs and uses the u.s. census bureau’s supplemental poverty measure, or spm. unlike the official poverty measure, the spm accounts for government benefits, taxes and geographic differences in expenses, including housing. pew says connecticut was among 10 states where above-average housing costs made up the largest shares of poverty, and connecticut tied for seventh in the study. that means the headline percentages are estimates from a model, not a count of residents who listed rent as the reason they became poor. the distinction matters for how the results should be read. pew researchers looked at what would happen if rents fell relative to the national average while other household costs stayed the same. in that hypothetical, a 20% decline in inflation-adjusted rents would lower the average poverty threshold for connecticut families with children by $3,905, according to the report. the exercise does not predict that rents will fall or promise that every family would see the same savings; it shows how strongly housing costs affect the income a household needs to remain above the spm line. connecticut public, which reported on the analysis monday, quoted pew housing-policy project director alex horowitz saying the state is in a “long-term landlords market,” with tenants competing for scarce homes. horowitz attributed that pressure to a shortage of housing and told the public broadcaster that the effect can blunt help from programs such as snap, housing choice vouchers and the low-income housing tax credit. when rent rises faster than a household’s resources, assistance can cover less of the family’s actual needs even if the benefit itself has not changed. the report’s policy argument is that reducing poverty requires attention to costs as well as income. pew points to zoning, building-code and permitting rules that can make it harder or more expensive to add homes. the analysis also cites examples in austin and minneapolis where inflation-adjusted rents fell by about 20% after changes intended to allow more housing. those examples do not establish that connecticut would see the same result, but they provide the comparison behind pew’s estimate that lower rents could reduce poverty by 18% to 26% and child poverty by 21% to 38% in the high-cost states it studied. horowitz told connecticut public that lawmakers could ease the pressure by making it possible to build smaller apartment buildings, reducing some lot-size requirements and allowing more townhomes, condominiums and apartments through zoning changes. he also said connecticut ranked 49th nationally in housing production per person from 2017 through 2023. that figure is a production comparison cited by the report’s local coverage, not a claim that every municipality has the same shortage or that new construction alone would immediately make every neighborhood affordable. the analysis does not settle several questions that will shape the state’s response. it does not identify which connecticut cities or towns account for the largest share of the housing-related poverty estimate, nor does it say how many homes would need to be built to produce a 20% statewide rent decline. it also does not remove the need for targeted aid: pew says the lowest-income households would still need vouchers and other subsidies even if rents fell. the study therefore presents housing production and direct assistance as complementary tools rather than substitutes. for connecticut families, the near-term effect is mainly political and practical. the findings give state and local officials a way to connect housing approvals, zoning rules and rental supply to poverty policy, while the spm framework offers a more realistic picture of costs than an income-only measure. the next test will be whether connecticut can add homes quickly enough, in places where people need them, without assuming that a statewide percentage automatically describes every renter’s experience. connecticut housing housing ct hartford connecticut connecticut housing poverty rents child poverty zoning housing supply

ct-husky-d-medicaid-work-rules-2026-10-0.text: connecticut prepares husky d enrollees for medicaid work rules starting jan. 1 state officials are promoting outreach and eligibility tools as new federal requirements threaten coverage for roughly 108,000 husky d enrollees who do not document work, training, education or an exemption. connecticut officials are trying to keep residents connected to husky d as new federal medicaid requirements approach, but the state has not committed to replacing federal money that could be lost. gov. ned lamont and state health officials gathered at stamford hospital on monday to explain the outreach effort ahead of rules that begin jan. 1. the event and the governor's position were reported by [ct mirror](https://ctmirror.org/2026/10/05/lamont-ct-response-to-medicaid-cuts/), while [wfsb](https://www.wfsb.com/2026/10/05/state-leaders-detail-plans-support-husky-health-d-recipients-ahead-new-rules/?outputtype=amp) previewed the state's plan and the timing of the announcement. the change applies to husky d, connecticut's medicaid coverage for low-income adults without dependent children. ct mirror reported that andrea barton reeves, commissioner of the department of social services, said the new federal law puts coverage for about 108,000 husky d residents at risk. that figure describes people who could be affected by the new rules; it does not mean all 108,000 will lose coverage. eligibility will depend on each person's work, income, education, community-service activity and qualifying exemptions. under the connecticut department of social services' [official h.r.1 guidance](https://portal.ct.gov/dss/all-programs/dss-benefits-and-hr1/hr1-for-members/hr1-work-rule-changes), an affected adult can satisfy the new rule by earning at least $580 a month, working at least 80 hours a month, completing at least 80 hours of community service, or taking part in an approved work or training program for at least 80 hours. enrollment at least half-time in an education program can also qualify. the guidance says combinations of qualifying activities may be used to reach 80 hours, so the rule is broader than a simple requirement to hold a conventional job. the same dss page lists categories that are exempt, including parents or caregiver relatives of a child under 14, pregnant or postpartum people, foster and former foster youth, american indian or alaska native people, certain veterans, and people who are medically frail. people recently released from jail or prison, people in drug or alcohol treatment, and some people experiencing a short-term hardship may also qualify for an exemption. the exemptions matter because a missed work-hour target does not by itself establish that someone is ineligible for husky d; the agency must apply the full eligibility rules to the person's circumstances. dss says it is building ways to confirm eligibility from records the state already has, a process commonly called ex parte verification. ct mirror reported that the department is using that approach to reduce the paperwork required from people whose information already demonstrates that they qualify. the state has also launched [medicaidmattersct.org](https://www.medicaidmattersct.org/) as an information resource. dss's h.r.1 materials direct residents to community action agencies for help understanding the new work rules and reporting qualifying hours. the policy debate is also about money. connecticut has used $115 million from an emergency response fund to help offset the expiration of federal subsidies for affordable care act plans, according to ct mirror. lamont said the state would first concentrate on helping eligible residents use the benefits that remain available and did not promise state dollars to replace the medicaid cuts. that leaves an unresolved question for lawmakers and the administration: whether connecticut will later spend state money to protect coverage for people who are eligible under current state rules but cannot meet the new federal conditions. for stamford, monday's event put the national medicaid changes in a local setting. the gathering included stamford mayor caroline simmons, stamford health officials and city health-and-human-services staff, according to wfsb. their role is primarily outreach: helping residents understand what will change, who may be exempt and what documents they may need. the event did not change the federal effective date or create a new coverage category. the immediate deadline is jan. 1, 2027, when the work and community-engagement rules take effect. the dss faq also says husky d adults will renew every six months instead of every 12 months beginning jan. 1, and applicants will face a shorter period of retroactive coverage. residents who rely on husky d should use the official dss guidance, respond to renewal notices and seek help from a community action agency before assuming that a new rule ends their coverage. the practical outcome will depend on how the state verifies exemptions, counts qualifying activity and handles people whose circumstances change during the transition. connecticut health health ct crash that closed southbound i-91 in windsor thursday evening. one person was seriously injured thursday evening after being thrown from a vehicle in a two-car crash on interstate 91 south in windsor, connecticut state police said. the collision closed a section of the highway during the evening commute and remained under investigation overnight. connecticut department of transportation officials said the crash was reported at about 5:15 p.m. between exits 36 and 35b. the agency reported the southbound closure while state police and emergency crews worked at the scene. the reported closure the person ejected from the vehicle was taken to hartford hospital by windsor emergency medical services with serious injuries. authorities did not release the person's name, age or condition beyond ct-leap-attendance-grants-2026-09-30.excerpt: The new grants expand a home-visiting program that state officials say helped drive four straight years of lower chronic absenteeism, but the latest awards will still have to translate into local services.
ct-leap-attendance-grants-2026-09-30.text: connecticut awards $6.2m to 29 districts to improve student attendance the new grants expand a home-visiting program that state officials say helped drive four straight years of lower chronic absenteeism, but the latest awards will still have to translate into local services. connecticut is awarding approximately $6.2 million to 29 school districts and regional education organizations for a home-visiting program aimed at bringing chronically absent students back into regular contact with their schools. the grants, announced sept. 30 by gov. ned lamont and education commissioner charlene russell-tucker, are being distributed through the learner engagement and attendance program, known as leap. the money comes from a $7 million state budget line item. about $800,000 will support statewide infrastructure such as home-visitor training, program implementation and data collection, according to the [connecticut governor’s announcement](https://portal.ct.gov/governor/news/press-releases/2026/09-2026/governor-lamont-and-commissioner-russell-tucker-announce-state-grants-to-expand-program). leap pairs trained school staff and community partners with students and families. the visits are intended to identify the practical or personal barriers behind missed school days and connect families with services that can make regular attendance possible. the program began in 2021 with federal pandemic-relief money, initially serving 15 districts. it later expanded to 25, and this round brings the state’s reach to 29 districts for the 2026-27 school year. the recipients include some of connecticut’s largest districts. waterbury is slated to receive $525,000, hartford $500,000, bridgeport $475,000 and new haven $425,000. stamford will receive $350,000, while smaller awards go to districts including east windsor, east haven, plainfield and jamestown. middletown’s $125,000 award was reported separately by [middletown patch](https://patch.com/connecticut/middletown-ct/middletown-school-system-getting-6-figure-grant-aimed-boosting-attendance), which described the grant as funding for the same statewide leap effort. state officials say connecticut’s chronic-absenteeism rate fell from 23.7% in the 2021-22 school year to 16.4% in 2025-26. the governor’s office calculated that change as nearly 35,000 more students attending school regularly than at the earlier point. the figures describe statewide movement and do not establish that leap alone caused the decline; the announcement calls the program one part of a broader attendance strategy. there is earlier research behind the state’s decision to continue the program. the center for connecticut education research collaboration, a partnership involving the state education department and connecticut colleges, studied leap’s first 15 districts. its [published evaluation](https://portal.ct.gov/ccerc/current-projects/leap) found attendance gains after home visits, including an average increase of nearly 15 percentage points six months after visits for students served during the 2021-22 school year. the study also reported different effects by grade level and district, which matters because the new grant round includes a broader mix of communities than the initial cohort. connecticut says home visitors have conducted about 88,000 visits and reached roughly 53,000 students since leap began. those totals are cumulative program figures supplied by the state, not an independent count released with the new awards. the current announcement also does not provide a district-by-district attendance target or a deadline for demonstrating results. the immediate test will be local execution. districts will need to recruit or assign visitors, train them, coordinate with community organizations and turn conversations with families into help with transportation, health, housing, counseling or other barriers when those needs are identified. if the grants produce lasting attendance gains, connecticut will have a stronger case for making the home-visiting model a durable part of school operations after the pandemic-era funding that launched it has faded. new-england new-england new england ct hartford connecticut connecticut student attendance chronic absenteeism leap public schools education funding

cheney brothers historic district and was built in 1886 as worker housing associated with the cheney brothers silk mills, according to testimony summarized in the report. the purchase was made for a goslin told the council that the house needs work but rated its underlying quality highly, and he suggested that manchester could sell it to a preservation-minded developer. he also described a possible compromise that would keep the house while removing the garage for about 10 spaces, although he warned that the resulting lot would be substandard. the dispute matters beyond one building agenda](https://portal.ct.gov/-/media/decd/historic-preservation/06_about_shpo/hpc-agendas/october-7-2026-hpc-meeting-agenda---final.pdf?rev=d3f872755d7d4d80b6608c3ebb09f353) separately placed 29-31 [connecticut public reporting republished by ct mirror](https://ctmirror.org/2026/07/09/manchester-net-zero-library/) described the new facility as a 75,000-square-foot, all-electric, net-zero-energy public library with solar arrays, battery storage and geothermal heating and cooling. the project was designed to address shortcomings at the older mary cheney library, including limited study, meeting and parking space. that context explains why manchester is pressing for additional parking, but it also means the preservation fight is testing whether a new civic facility can expand without sacrificing a historic resource next door. the next decision belongs to the attorney general’s office, which will review materials from the council before deciding whether to begin a legal process, according to ct insider. the council’s vote is not itself a final court order, and the available public reports do not establish whether demolition work has been scheduled or whether the town will revise its plan. for now, the unresolved questions are whether the home can be preserved or adaptively reused, whether fewer parking spaces can meet the library’s needs, and whether the state will seek a formal intervention before manchester moves forward. connecticut preservation preservation ct manchester 29-31 eldridge street, manchester, connecticut connecticut manchester historic preservation libraries parking cheney brothers historic district development

ct-middletown-veterans-cemetery-expansio.excerpt: A $584,250 federal grant, paired with $294,250 in state money, will help Connecticut expand its only state-operated veterans cemetery as cremation burial space nears capacity.
ct-middletown-veterans-cemetery-expansio.text: middletown veterans cemetery expansion will add 1,510 cremation plots a $584,250 federal grant, paired with $294,250 in state money, will help connecticut expand its only state-operated veterans cemetery as cremation burial space nears capacity. connecticut will expand the state veterans cemetery in middletown with 1,510 new burial plots for cremated remains, state officials announced friday. the project will use a $584,250 grant from the u.s. department of veterans affairs alongside $294,250 that connecticut has already allocated, adding capacity at a cemetery that serves veterans and eligible family members from across the state. the [governor’s announcement](https://portal.ct.gov/governor/news/press-releases/2026/10-2026/governor-lamont-announces-funding-to-expand-the-connecticut-state-veterans-cemetery-in-middletown) was also covered locally by [middletown patch](https://patch.com/connecticut/middletown-ct/middletown-veterans-cemetery-expansion-add-cremation-burial-plots). the work is planned for a parcel next to the existing cemetery at 317 bow lane. the property was formerly used by connecticut valley hospital and was recently transferred from the state department of mental health and addiction services to the department of veterans affairs, which is overseeing the expansion. the location allows the state to extend an existing cemetery rather than wait for a separate site to be developed. under the state’s announcement, the federal money will pay for the cremains burial plots and related site work, including an entrance gate, fencing, landscaping, irrigation components, concrete-block storage bays, site furnishings and supporting infrastructure. the state funding will support demolition of cottage 22, a vacant connecticut valley hospital building on the property. connecticut has not announced a completion date for the construction. the expansion is aimed at a specific capacity problem. the [connecticut department of veterans affairs](https://portal.ct.gov/dva/cemetery-and-memorial-services) says the middletown cemetery currently has 14,718 burial plots and 3,000 columbarium niches. state officials estimate that the existing supply of in-ground cremation plots will be exhausted around january 2028 without additional space; with the expansion, those plots are projected to remain available through at least december 2033. that timing matters because the cemetery offers several distinct choices for families. the project concerns in-ground burial of cremated remains, while casket burials and above-ground columbarium niches are separate options. the state says extending the cremation-plot supply through 2033 would bring the estimated depletion dates for all three options into alignment, giving officials time to plan a future cemetery intended to serve veterans and their families over the longer term. the middletown site was established in 1985 and is the largest state-operated veterans cemetery in connecticut, according to the department of veterans affairs. the department’s [cemetery-services page](https://portal.ct.gov/dva/cemetery-and-memorial-services) says the site is the final resting place for more than 16,000 veterans and family members. connecticut also maintains the colonel raymond f. gates cemetery in rocky hill, which is reserved primarily for veterans residing at the state’s residential and skilled-nursing facilities, and provides perpetual care for spring grove veterans cemetery in darien, which is closed to new burials. the funding announcement follows a longer state effort to secure land and keep the middletown facility eligible for federal cemetery support. a [2023 state bond authorization](https://portal.ct.gov/-/media/opm/bud-capital-budget/agendas/cy-2023/agenda%5fdec15%5f2023.pdf) set aside $3 million for land acquisition and improvements connected to the department of veterans affairs cemetery program. a subsequent state planning document said the middletown cemetery was expected to approach capacity within several years, while an [environmental scoping notice](https://portal.ct.gov/ceq/das/scoping-notice/dva-cemetery-expansion) identified the bow lane expansion area and estimated that existing space could be depleted in about 4.6 years. for connecticut veterans’ families, the immediate result is a planned increase in local burial capacity, not a new benefit or completed construction project. the state and federal awards still have to be translated into demolition, site preparation and cemetery improvements. the announcement does not specify the construction schedule or the final operating date for the new plots. the department of veterans affairs will remain responsible for project oversight and for coordinating burial services while the expansion proceeds. connecticut veterans veterans ct ct-new-haven-quantumct-hub-opening-2026-.excerpt: The 4,500-square-foot center at 101 College Street will connect Yale and UConn researchers with students, startups and industry as the state builds a quantum-technology corridor.
ct-new-haven-quantumct-hub-opening-2026-.text: new haven opens quantumct hub as connecticut bets on quantum-tech economy the 4,500-square-foot center at 101 college street will connect yale and uconn researchers with students, startups and industry as the state builds a quantum-technology corridor. a new research and startup hub opened tuesday night in downtown new haven, giving connecticut’s long-running quantum-technology effort a physical base for collaboration among universities, entrepreneurs and industry. the ribbon-cutting at 101 college street marked the opening of a 4,500-square-foot center operated by quantumct, a nonprofit created to help move quantum research toward commercial uses. the [new haven independent report published by ct mirror](https://ctmirror.org/2026/10/07/quantumct-innovation-hub-new-haven-101-college/) said the first-floor space is intended for researchers, students and entrepreneurs. its practical role is less about housing a finished quantum computer than about creating a place where people can share research, train workers, develop partnerships and build companies. a planned project at nearby 2 church street is expected to provide additional room for companies that grow out of the broader innovation district, but that facility is not the same as the hub that opened this week. the initiative joins two different connecticut strengths. yale researchers have built a long record in quantum information processing, while the university of connecticut has developed a research group focused in part on quantum sensing, according to the ct mirror report. uconn said in a july account of the federal award that about 65 of its researchers were working in quantum-related areas, with that number expected to rise to 70. quantum sensing uses unusual properties of matter at very small scales to measure things such as temperature, distance and magnetic fields with exceptional sensitivity. the new center also gives a local address to a funding strategy that has grown rapidly. the national science foundation [listed connecticut’s quantum technologies engine](https://www.nsf.gov/news/nsf-awards-12-new-regional-innovation-engines-fuel-research) among 12 new regional innovation engines announced in july. nsf said each team would initially receive $15 million over two years, with the possibility of as much as $160 million over a decade if it meets defined milestones. the connecticut team is led by uconn and is built around a coalition that includes universities, nonprofits and private-sector partners. state officials have made a separate, sizable commitment. uconn reported that connecticut pledged $61 million to support a quantum corridor headquartered in new haven, while the governor’s broader downtown investment announcement described a $50.5 million innovation-cluster package for infrastructure and facilities. the figures refer to overlapping parts of a multiyear strategy rather than a single check delivered at tuesday’s ceremony. a [new haven board of alders record](https://newhaven-ct.legistar.com/legislationdetail.aspx?fulltext=1&guid=f6aa0ae3-8682-4c53-8b30-9167845acacb&id=8045400&options=&search=) describes the city’s role in an innovation cluster linking quantum technology, bioscience, artificial intelligence and advanced computing. that public investment is meant to solve a familiar problem in emerging technology: strong research does not automatically produce local companies, skilled workers or durable jobs. quantumct’s model puts academic researchers, students and potential employers in the same network and gives early-stage businesses a place to find partners. the state’s own record describes the goal as supporting research and development, entrepreneurship and the translation of discoveries into products and services; those are objectives, not evidence that the corridor has already delivered a particular number of jobs or companies. private investment is beginning to test whether the strategy can work. the ct mirror report noted that d-wave acquired yale-founded quantum circuits for $550 million earlier this year and that d-wave is considering expanding the new haven workforce. that transaction is a company decision, not a guarantee for the region, but it illustrates why state and university leaders see a connection between basic research and commercial infrastructure as important. the hub is designed to shorten that distance without claiming that every research project will become a business. for new haven, the immediate change is visible and concrete: a new shared space in the downtown bioscience district, alongside a growing cluster of laboratories and offices. for students and workers elsewhere in connecticut, the longer-term question is whether the investment creates accessible training and jobs beyond the universities. for taxpayers, the relevant test will be whether quantumct meets the federal benchmarks attached to the nsf award and whether the state’s facilities support companies that can remain in connecticut. the opening therefore marks a beginning, not a finished quantum economy. quantumct still has to build its research, workforce and business networks, and the nsf funding can expand only if the initiative meets its milestones. connecticut now has a headquarters, a federal award and a substantial state-backed plan; the next measure of success will be what ct-new-haven-yale-police-firearm-dischar.excerpt: The weapon did not strike the person inside the locked car, who was critically hurt while self-harming; Connecticut’s inspector general is investigating the response.
ct-new-haven-yale-police-firearm-dischar.text: yale police firearm discharges during new haven rescue attempt, officials say the weapon did not strike the person inside the locked car, who was critically hurt while self-harming; connecticut’s inspector general is investigating the response. a yale police officer’s firearm discharged wednesday morning while the officer was trying to reach a person who was self-harming inside a locked car in new haven, according to yale officials, mayor justin elicker and separate local television reports. the person was not hit by the gunfire but was taken to yale new haven hospital in critical condition with injuries described by officials as self-inflicted. the incident unfolded at about 9:21 a.m. in the new haven yale club parking lot behind 205 whitney avenue, elicker told [nbc connecticut](https://www.nbcconnecticut.com/news/local/yale/3784890/). yale police responded after receiving a report involving a person inside the vehicle. a yale alert issued around 9:40 a.m. said there was no threat to the wider community, according to [patch](https://patch.com/connecticut/newhaven/new-haven-police-investigating-incident-205-whitney-avenue-street-closed-yale). duane lovello, yale’s head of public safety, said in a statement that the officer saw the person attempting to harm themselves and tried to intervene. the vehicle was locked. as the officer attempted to break the window with the firearm, the weapon discharged, lovello said. after the person was removed, the officer began medical aid before emergency medical personnel arrived, according to the account reported by nbc connecticut and [wfsb](https://www.wfsb.com/2026/10/14/police-investigate-scene-whitney-avenue-new-haven/). the available reporting does not establish precisely how the weapon discharged or whether the firearm contacted the glass before firing. it does establish that the person inside the vehicle was not struck by the round. elicker said the person appeared to be stabbing themselves when the officer arrived, and nbc connecticut reported that surgery was underway wednesday morning. the person’s identity and further medical details were not released. the responding yale officer was also undergoing a medical evaluation, lovello said. the new haven police department and yale police department were assisting at the scene, while connecticut’s office of the state inspector general took over the investigation. wfsb reported that the inspector general’s involvement is required when a police officer discharges a weapon in a use-of-force incident, and that body-worn-camera video was expected to be released in the following days. whitney avenue was closed between sachem street and humphrey street while investigators worked near the yale club, affecting traffic and access to nearby buildings. yale’s initial public alert asked people to avoid the area, but the reports did not describe an ongoing threat to students, employees or residents. the closure and response also led the mayor to cancel a scheduled briefing about the lower state street redesign project, according to patch. the episode raises two separate questions that remain unresolved: what led the person to the vehicle and exactly how the officer’s firearm discharged during the rescue attempt. those questions are now part of the inspector general’s review, and the initial accounts do not announce any finding of wrongdoing. the investigation is also expected to clarify the officer’s actions, the timing of the medical response and what the camera footage shows. for new haven, the incident is both a public-safety investigation and a mental-health emergency response that happened in a busy area near yale’s campus. yale said it was thinking of everyone involved as they received medical care. nbc connecticut also included information for people in crisis: anyone who may be at immediate risk can call or text 988, the suicide and crisis lifeline. no additional details about the patient, the officer or the investigation had been released by wednesday evening. connecticut public-safety public safety ct new haven 205 whitney avenue, new haven, connecticut connecticut new haven yale ct-prediction-markets-exit-crackdown-202.excerpt: State officials say three of nine companies targeted over unlicensed sports wagering have stopped offering prediction-market services in Connecticut, but the scope of at least one departure remains disputed.
ct-prediction-markets-exit-crackdown-202.text: three prediction-market operators halt connecticut sports contracts amid state crackdown state officials say three of nine companies targeted over unlicensed sports wagering have stopped offering prediction-market services in connecticut, but the scope of at least one departure remains disputed. connecticut regulators say three of the nine prediction-market operators targeted in the state's september crackdown have stopped offering sports-event contracts to residents, giving the state's campaign against a fast-growing form of online wagering its first reported retreat. the development affects platforms that let users buy and sell contracts tied to sports outcomes, while leaving six other named operators in communication with the department of consumer protection. the [connecticut office of the governor](https://portal.ct.gov/governor/news/press-releases/2026/09-2026/governor-lamont-announces-new-actions-against-illegal-prediction-markets-offering-sports-wagers) said the department of consumer protection issued nine cease-and-desist orders in september. the agency's list included polymarket, coinbase, crypto.com, robinhood, prophetx, novig, webull, gemini and underdog predict. the orders directed the platforms to stop advertising, promoting or making unlicensed online gambling available to connecticut residents. they also required the platforms to let connecticut customers withdraw funds held on their services. the new development was reported by connecticut news outlets after dcp commissioner bryan cafferelli said three operators had heard the state's message and were leaving. [ct insider reported](https://www.ctinsider.com/politics/article/prediction-market-companies-leave-ct-22460358.php) that officials identified the three as prophetx, gemini and webull. the story said the department remained in contact with polymarket, coinbase, crypto.com, robinhood, novig and underdog. a related [news-times report](https://www.newstimes.com/politics/article/connecticut-prediction-market-companies-leave-ct-22460358.php) clarified that webull intended to continue its other services in connecticut and was responding specifically to the order concerning prediction markets. that distinction matters because “leaving connecticut” can describe several different actions: shutting down a company's entire business in the state, removing only sports contracts, or restricting particular products through geolocation. the news-times report said an analyst disputed the characterization of prophetx's withdrawal, while webull said it was still operating other services. the public statements reviewed for this report therefore support a narrower conclusion: state officials say three operators have stopped or are stopping the targeted sports-market activity, but the exact product-by-product status is not independently established for every company. connecticut's position is that sports prediction markets are wagers, not investments insulated from state gaming rules. the governor's september announcement said the state believes the contracts can take bets from people under 21, people on the voluntary self-exclusion list and participants wagering on connecticut college sports. officials also said the platforms do not operate under the technical, integrity and consumer-protection standards required of licensed sportsbooks. those are the state's allegations and regulatory conclusions; the companies have argued that their event contracts are financial products governed by federal law. the fight has regional and national significance because prediction markets have expanded beyond election-style questions into contracts on game winners, point spreads and player statistics. connecticut's release said one platform reported nearly $250 million in college-football trading volume on the first day of the 2026 season. the state is trying to preserve a more limited legal market created in 2021, when connecticut authorized sports wagering through licensed partners connected to draftkings, fanduel and fanatics, while maintaining an age minimum and responsible-gambling rules. the enforcement campaign also sits alongside a court dispute. connecticut sued kalshi in august seeking to block what the attorney general described as unlicensed sports betting. in its [august 26 announcement](https://portal.ct.gov/ag/press-releases/2026-press-releases/connecticut-sues-kalshi-to-stop-illegal-unlicensed-sports-betting), the attorney general's office said a federal judge had denied kalshi's request for a preliminary injunction and that kalshi had appealed to the second circuit. the kalshi litigation is separate from the september orders to the nine operators, but it could help determine how far state gambling laws reach when a platform describes its products as federally regulated event contracts. for connecticut users, the immediate practical question is access to specific sports markets and the ability to withdraw money, not whether all prediction-market products have disappeared. the department said it is still communicating with six operators, and the state has not announced a final resolution with each of them. further cease-and-desist actions, company notices, court rulings or public compliance records will be needed to show whether the remaining platforms restrict their sports offerings or continue to challenge connecticut's interpretation of state law. connecticut gambling gambling ct hartford connecticut ct-realpage-rent-pricing-case-2026-10-06.excerpt: A federal antitrust lawsuit backed by Connecticut and other states survived RealPage's effort to have the case thrown out, keeping allegations about algorithmic rent setting in court.
ct-realpage-rent-pricing-case-2026-10-06.text: connecticut realpage rent-pricing case will continue after court ruling a federal antitrust lawsuit backed by connecticut and other states survived realpage's effort to have the case thrown out, keeping allegations about algorithmic rent setting in court. connecticut's antitrust case against realpage will continue after a court rejected the company's attempt to have the rent-pricing lawsuit thrown out, attorney general william tong's office announced tuesday. the ruling keeps alive a multistate challenge to software that prosecutors say helped landlords use nonpublic market information to coordinate apartment prices. the [connecticut office of the attorney general](https://portal.ct.gov/ag/press-releases/2026-press-releases/court-sides-with-attorney-general-tong-in-realpage-case) said connecticut, the u.s. department of justice and other states sued realpage in 2024. the case alleges that realpage sold revenue-management software to property managers, collected sensitive information about rents, discounts and available units, and used that information to recommend prices. state officials further allege that the system encouraged property managers to accept recommendations automatically, reducing the incentive to compete for renters. those are allegations, not findings that realpage or the landlords violated the law. the ruling is a decision about whether the claims can proceed, not a final judgment on liability or a determination that any particular connecticut tenant was overcharged. realpage has not been found liable in the state announcement, and the public release did not identify the judge or provide a full copy of the order. the litigation also includes six large landlord defendants named in a january 2025 amended complaint: greystar real estate partners, blackstone's livcor, camden property trust, cushman & wakefield, pinnacle property management services and willow bridge property company. the attorney general's office said the coalition alleges those companies worked with realpage and each other by sharing competitively sensitive information and using common pricing tools. a prior state announcement identified greystar, pinnacle and willow bridge as companies operating in connecticut, giving the case a direct connection to renters in the state. two of those landlord matters have already taken a different path. tong's office said connecticut joined other attorneys general in settlements totaling $7 million with livcor and $7 million with greystar. under those agreements, the companies agreed to stop using nonpublic data from other landlords to set rents. the settlements do not resolve the remaining case against realpage or answer the broader question of how algorithmic pricing affects apartment markets. the [justice department's case page](https://www.justice.gov/atr/case/us-and-plaintiff-states-v-realpage-inc) identifies the case as *u.s. and plaintiff states v. realpage, inc.* and lists connecticut among the state plaintiffs. its docket materials include the 2024 complaint, an amended complaint and filings related to proposed judgments involving several landlord defendants. the federal record shows the case has generated separate resolutions and ongoing claims rather than one single proceeding with one outcome for every defendant. the dispute matters in connecticut because rent-setting decisions can affect the starting price, renewal price and discounts offered at multifamily properties, even when the software company and property owner are not household names to tenants. the state's case does not establish how much any connecticut renter paid because of the alleged conduct, and the attorney general's announcement did not provide a statewide damages estimate. it does show what the state is seeking: an order preventing realpage and participating property managers from sharing nonpublic information and working together to inflate rents. renters should not treat the tuesday ruling as an immediate rent reduction or a payment announcement. a surviving lawsuit can move into further litigation, settlement discussions or trial, and the public sources reviewed for this report do not establish a final remedy or timeline. for now, connecticut remains one of the states pursuing the case, while the next major developments will come through court filings, additional settlements or a final decision on the allegations. connecticut housing housing ct hartford connecticut connecticut housing rent antitrust realpage

ct-recreational-trails-grants-2026-10-01.excerpt: The grants will support construction, accessibility work, planning and maintenance, with half of the selected projects serving distressed municipalities or environmental-justice communities.
ct-recreational-trails-grants-2026-10-01.text: connecticut awards $10.5m for 50 recreational-trail projects the grants will support construction, accessibility work, planning and maintenance, with half of the selected projects serving distressed municipalities or environmental-justice communities. connecticut is awarding approximately $10.5 million to 50 projects intended to build, repair, connect and improve recreational trails across the state, gov. ned lamont and the department of energy and environmental protection announced thursday. the awards come through the connecticut recreational trails grant program after a competitive review by deep and the connecticut greenways council. the money was previously allocated by the state bond commission, according to the [governor’s announcement](https://portal.ct.gov/governor/news/press-releases/2026/10-2026/governor-lamont-announces-state-grants-for-recreational-trails). the program supports more than new stretches of pavement: the 2026 list includes construction, rehabilitation, bridge replacement, accessibility upgrades, trailhead and parking improvements, planning and design, equipment, outreach and long-term maintenance. that mix means the award will produce different kinds of results in different communities. winchester received $749,000 for construction intended to complete the sue grossman still river greenway. new haven received $274,730 for planning and design at the east rock park college woods inclusive community trail, while naugatuck received $400,000 to design a connector for the naugatuck river greenway between naugatuck and waterbury. bridgeport received $180,000 for planning and design of the old mill green pathways project, and east hartford received $200,000 to design a gap closure on the east coast greenway. the geographic spread is one reason the grants matter beyond individual trailheads. other awards include $505,000 for a multi-use connector in avon, $495,000 for an accessible bridge and trail at steep rock association’s hidden valley preserve, $492,874 for the university of connecticut’s trails and active-living program, and $498,400 for the connecticut forest and park association’s blue-blazed trail system and woodland conservation corps. the full award table also includes projects in eastern connecticut, the shoreline, the hartford region and the northwest hills. twenty-five of the 50 projects are in, or serve, municipalities the state classifies as distressed or environmental-justice communities. that designation does not mean every project has the same scope or construction schedule, but it signals that the review process gave weight to communities that have not always had equal access to outdoor recreation. the state says the awards are designed to improve public access while supporting recreation, active transportation, conservation and local connections. there is already evidence of substantial demand for the network. connecticut’s trail census, a uconn program that uses infrared counters and volunteer-supported data collection, recorded more than 2.7 million trail uses at 27 monitored locations during 2025, the state release said. the [uconn ct trails program](https://cttrails.uconn.edu/) maintains the census and a public trail-finder system; its 2025 count report is listed in the program’s [research archive](https://cttrails.uconn.edu/pubs/reports/). counter totals measure recorded uses at monitored sites, not every trip on every trail, so they should be read as an indicator rather than a statewide attendance total. the program also arrives as connecticut continues to treat trails as public-health and economic infrastructure. deep describes more than 2,000 miles of multi-use trails in state parks and forests alone, while the governor’s office said outdoor recreation contributes about $6 billion annually to the state economy and supports more than 50,000 jobs. those figures come from state and federal economic accounts cited in the announcement, not from an independent assessment of this grant round. the next phase will be local implementation. planning awards still require design work, permits and decisions about routes, access and maintenance before construction can begin. construction awards will need to be matched with contracting, scheduling and long-term upkeep. for residents, the practical question is when each town or organization can turn its award into a safer crossing, a more accessible trail, a completed connection or a maintained public route. the grant list provides the funding commitments; project timelines will depend on the recipients and the state’s agreement process. new-england new-england new england ct hartford connecticut connecticut recreational trails deep outdoor recreation public access infrastructure

ct-revolution-wind-permit-review-2026-10.excerpt: The Interior Department wants a judge to send the project’s three-year-old approval back for review even as the nearly completed wind farm is already supplying power to New England.
ct-revolution-wind-permit-review-2026-10.text: federal bid to revisit revolution wind permit puts connecticut project back in court the interior department wants a judge to send the project’s three-year-old approval back for review even as the nearly completed wind farm is already supplying power to new england. the trump administration is asking a federal judge to send the approval for revolution wind back to the interior department for another review, reopening a fight over connecticut’s first offshore wind project as the 65-turbine farm nears full operation. the request does not itself cancel the project or order its turbines offline, but it creates a new legal uncertainty around a facility that is already producing electricity for the regional grid. the department of justice made the request in a friday, oct. 9, filing in a lawsuit brought by green oceans, a rhode island-based group that challenges federal approvals for revolution wind and the south fork wind project. [ct mirror reported](https://ctmirror.org/2026/10/13/trump-administration-seeks-to-rescind-approval-for-revolution-wind/) that interior is seeking remand of the project’s construction and operations plan approval so the agency can reevaluate whether its review complied with the outer continental shelf lands act. remand would return the approval to the agency for further consideration; it is not the same as a final court ruling that the project’s permit is invalid. connecticut officials responded wednesday by saying the filing conflicts with the administration’s stated interest in faster energy permitting. in an [official statement](https://portal.ct.gov/governor/news/press-releases/2026/10-2026/governor-lamont-on-trump-administration-attempt-to-block-new-energy-sources), gov. ned lamont, attorney general william tong and deep acting commissioner emma cimino said they were reviewing their options with project developer ørsted. tong said the state would be prepared to return to court to protect connecticut jobs and access to the project’s power. the dispute is significant because revolution wind is no longer only a proposal. the [connecticut governor’s office](https://portal.ct.gov/governor/news/press-releases/2026/10-2026/governor-lamont-on-trump-administration-attempt-to-block-new-energy-sources) says the 704-megawatt project is about 15 nautical miles southeast of point judith, rhode island, began construction in 2023 and received its 65th and final turbine in september. the project has begun supplying power, and state officials expect full commercial operation later this year. ørsted’s onshore assembly work has used the state pier in new london, tying the federal dispute to connecticut’s port, construction workforce and power customers even though the turbines stand offshore. at full output, the project is expected to generate enough electricity for about 350,000 homes across new england. connecticut is contracted to receive 304 megawatts, while rhode island is set to receive the remaining 400 megawatts, according to the state release. connecticut officials say the state’s share would cover about 5% of its electricity demand. deep estimates that, by 2028, the project could reduce electricity-market costs for connecticut and new england ratepayers by roughly $500 million a year and save connecticut customers $150 million to $200 million in public-benefit charges over the contract’s 20-year life. those are agency estimates, not guaranteed savings, and depend on the project reaching the expected operating schedule. the latest filing follows earlier attempts to stop construction. a federal judge allowed work to resume after the administration issued stop-work orders tied to national-security concerns, and the [sabin center’s case summary](https://www.climatecasechart.com/collections/revolution-wind-llc-v-burgum%5f6ce6) records that the court granted preliminary relief to the developer and the states in january. the new request instead focuses on whether the original construction-and-operations-plan review adequately addressed the federal law governing uses of the outer continental shelf, according to ct mirror and [canary media’s account of the filing](https://www.canarymedia.com/articles/offshore-wind/trump-reevaluate-permit-revolution-wind-orsted). canary media reported that the filing does not immediately change the project’s construction or generation while the judge considers the request. the court could reject the remand, allow the agency to reconsider the approval, or set additional briefing and conditions; the timing and eventual outcome remain unresolved. the interior department told ct mirror that it was following a briefing schedule and said the filing should not be read as a policy change, while connecticut’s officials argue that reopening an approval after construction is nearly complete undermines the certainty needed for major energy infrastructure. for new england, the next concrete step is a decision from u.s. district judge royce lamberth in the district of columbia case. until then, revolution wind remains a permitted, nearly completed project with power already reaching the grid, but its final transition to full commercial operation is proceeding under a fresh legal challenge. the state’s response also signals that connecticut may again ask the court to protect the project if the federal review threatens the construction schedule, the contracted electricity or the economic benefits officials associate with the wind farm. connecticut energy energy ct-shore-line-east-service-expansion-202.excerpt: The expanded CTrail schedule adds afternoon and evening trips between New Haven and New London, including a connection for riders arriving from New York.
ct-shore-line-east-service-expansion-202.text: shore line east adds four weekday trains as new schedule begins the expanded ctrail schedule adds afternoon and evening trips between new haven and new london, including a connection for riders arriving from new york. ctrail shore line east’s expanded weekday schedule began monday, adding four trains between new haven and new london and shortening some of the long gaps that have shaped travel along connecticut’s shoreline. the change affects commuters and other riders using stations from new haven to southeastern connecticut, with new afternoon and evening options in both directions. the new schedule adds two eastbound trains from new haven union station to new london. train 1628 leaves at 2:55 p.m. and reaches new london at 4:05 p.m.; train 1640 leaves at 6:03 p.m. and arrives at 7:13 p.m., according to the [official shore line east schedule effective oct. 5](https://shorelineeast.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/sle-october-5th-schedule_edit.pdf). both trains serve the line’s stations, including branford, guilford, madison, clinton, westbrook and old saybrook. two new westbound trains fill part of the return-trip gap. train 1683 departs new london at 4:40 p.m. and reaches new haven union station at 5:49 p.m. train 1693 leaves new london at 7:28 p.m. and arrives in new haven at 8:37 p.m. the official timetable also shows several existing trains with adjusted numbers or times, so a rider who remembers an older departure should check the current schedule rather than rely on the previous timetable. the 6:03 p.m. eastbound trip is especially relevant to passengers connecting from the new haven line. the new timetable lists a connection from metro-north super express train 3542, which leaves new york’s grand central terminal at 4:11 p.m. and stamford at 4:55 p.m. before reaching new haven. connecticut officials had described the connection as a way to make an evening trip toward the shoreline more practical, but the state’s schedule warns that connecting-service times are not guaranteed. the service increase follows an additional $3 million for the connecticut department of transportation in budget adjustments approved during the 2026 legislative session, according to [gov. ned lamont’s announcement](https://portal.ct.gov/governor/news/press-releases/2026/09-2026/governor-lamont-announces-additional-shore-line-east-rail-service-coming-on-october-5). the governor’s office said the schedule was shaped by customer-satisfaction survey responses and feedback to train and customer-service staff. the goal was to target periods when riders had fewer choices, not to redesign the line’s route or add new stations. the expansion is meaningful because shore line east remains below its pre-pandemic service and ridership levels. the [new haven register reported](https://www.nhregister.com/connecticut/article/ct-shore-line-east-more-trains-amtrak-22422965.php) that the four additions bring the line to 24 weekday trains, compared with 36 before the pandemic, and that ridership was about 247,000 last year versus roughly 660,000 in 2019. those figures provide context for the change: the new trips improve the timetable without restoring the line to its earlier frequency. shore line east connects new haven with new london and stops at state street and union station in new haven, as well as branford, guilford, madison, clinton, westbrook, old saybrook and new london. the corridor serves shoreline communities that rely on rail for work, school, medical appointments and connections to the broader new haven and new york markets. the added evening departures may be most useful to people whose schedules do not fit the older midday gaps or the limited late-day choices. the line’s operator says passengers should use the interactive trip planner or current timetable before traveling, particularly when connecting to metro-north or amtrak. the published schedule notes that amtrak trains listed for shore line east accept only a ctrail monthly pass or ten-trip ticket, and passengers must reserve a seat through amtrak’s ridereserve program. the immediate test for the expansion will be whether the new trips make those connection windows dependable enough to bring more riders back to the corridor. connecticut transportation transportation ct new haven shore line east corridor, connecticut connecticut shore line east ctrail commuter rail new haven new london transportation

ct-south-windsor-flock-camera-removal-20.excerpt: The Town Council voted 6-3 to take down eight automated license-plate readers within 60 days and purge the data, putting privacy concerns ahead of keeping the system as a police tool.
ct-south-windsor-flock-camera-removal-20.text: south windsor votes to end flock contract and remove license-plate readers the town council voted 6-3 to take down eight automated license-plate readers within 60 days and purge the data, putting privacy concerns ahead of keeping the system as a police tool. south windsor will end its contract with flock safety and remove the town’s automated license-plate readers after the town council voted 6-3 monday night. the resolution calls for the town manager to terminate the agreement, take down the readers within 60 days and purge the data collected through the system, according to the [journal inquirer’s report](https://www.ctinsider.com/journalinquirer/article/south-windsor-ct-flock-cameras-removed-22465434.php). the decision followed an oct. 5 public hearing on the eight cameras. the journal inquirer reported that residents from south windsor and neighboring communities spoke in favor of removal, with privacy and fourth amendment concerns dominating the testimony. no one at the hearing spoke in favor of keeping the system, the newspaper reported. a council straw poll after the hearing produced a 20-2 vote for removal, although the formal council action was the 6-3 vote that sets the town’s policy. mayor craig zimmerman said he initially supported the program but changed his position after meeting with officials inside and outside south windsor. he told the journal inquirer that the cameras could help police, but that he was not comfortable with the contract’s limits on control and accountability for the data. deputy mayor andrew paterna similarly framed the vote as a question about mass surveillance rather than distrust of south windsor police. the three council members who opposed removal emphasized the public-safety value of the technology. councilor audrey delnicki described flock and similar systems as another tool available to law enforcement, while councilor michael ouellette said he trusted the police chief and department to handle the data appropriately, according to the journal inquirer. councilor elizabeth pendleton said she was initially undecided before voting to remove the cameras because a private company operated the system and had access to extensive personal data. south windsor’s own april 6 council minutes show how the system was designed to work before monday’s vote. police chief kristian lindstrom described four bidirectional locations that scanned roadways in both directions and said the system had been operating for nearly 11 months. the minutes say ordinary data was stored for 30 days unless it was retained longer for an investigation, and that officers used individual accounts with trackable credentials. those details came from a presentation months before the council chose to end the program, not from an audit of the vote or a finding that south windsor officers misused the system. the [town minutes](https://www.southwindsor-ct.gov/sites/g/files/vyhlif8416/f/minutes/4-6-26_minutes-town-council-regular-meeting_2.pdf) provide that earlier official account. the local decision arrives as
